content.rendered:
One of the smallest canvases in the history of advertising, matchbox labels were produced economically and at high volume. Varying in size from a postage stamp to a playing card, these modest formats demanded maximum visual clarity. The designers had to reduce ideas to flat colour, simple iconography, and type that could be read at a glance. The printing constraints were severe. Most labels were produced by lithography, often in limited colour runs and on cheap paper stock. This forced designers to produce refined and constrained graphic design in the industrial era.

The first friction match is believed to have been sold in 1827, following several prototypes developed by John Walker, a pharmacist from Stockton-on-Tees. As matches spread across the world, so did the labels that housed them. By the mid-nineteenth century, match manufacture had become a significant industry, with factories across Europe, Asia, and America producing matches by the billion. With competition between manufacturers, the label was one of the few points of difference available. Like all packaging, it had to identify the brand, communicate safety information, and catch the eye, all within a rectangle small enough to fit in a pocket.

Among the highest-output producers, Czechoslovakia, the Soviet Union, and India each developed their own distinct visual styles. Most of my collected labels are from Czechoslovakia. They are often illustrated with depictions of people and animals rendered with strong, direct graphic messaging. Soviet labels were often used to advertise places such as destinations, regions, landmarks or achievements and have a vivid illustrative quality that makes them feel like travel posters shrunk in size. Indian labels seem brighter, frequently featuring wildlife such as tigers and elephants alongside religious iconography, reflecting a commercial print culture with its own visual language. British labels leaned toward the heraldic and typographic, strong brand identities, bold and legible, with less emphasis on illustration.

Nearly all the labels I have collected carry no indication of who designed them, though many state the manufacturer or label printer. These seem to be anonymous commissions produced under tight constraints (although they must be documented somewhere). Labels have since become highly collectable, and the hobby of collecting them is known as phillumeny. The collecting has attracted enthusiasts of all ages, much like stamp collecting does. Like stamps, they are small documents of graphic and social history. Here is a fraction of the thousands I have collected.

title.rendered: Examples of Czech Typography from 1909, Typografia

content.rendered:
As I have collected more issues of Typografia, I have been visually learning about the advancement and stylistic development of Typography in the Czech Republic. I have scanned in a few hundred samples of the inserted sheets. Most of them have never surfaced on the internet or ever had presence in design books, so it gives me great satisfaction to have these fantastic typographic pieces of history documented.

From the 1909 issues, I have scanned in at high-resolution sixty of the sample sheets from this (twentieth) volume. I have also scanned in lots more for future articles too.

 

Knihtiskaři Novotný a Příhoda business stationery and printed matter specimens from Královské Vinohrady, Prague. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, 1909. The designs feature ornamental typography and stylised Secession motifs integrated into practical commercial design.

 

Keramická továrna Praha–Nusle advertising specimen for a ceramic factory in Prague-Nusle. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, 1909. The composition balances geometric borders with a central female portrait, combining Viennese Secession influences with early modern Czech commercial design.

 

Bradáč commercial printing specimen for a Prague bookbinding and paper goods manufacturer. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 2, 1909. Designed and executed by Alois Chvály and printed by Fr. Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague. The design uses a rigid vertical structure, repeated modular ornament, and muted colour, quite like a style of early Art Deco.

 

Maison de Chapeaux Hanna Kreisingerova invoice and business stationery design for a Prague hat shop. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 2, 1909. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by Fr. Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague. The elegant script lettering with illustrated fashion imagery, reflect the fashionable commercial aesthetics of Czech Secession design.

 

Pravidla sazby typografické promotional page for a publication on typographic composition issued by the Typografia association in Prague. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 2, 1909. Designed by Karel Dyrink and printed by Slavoj Malý at the Politika printing works in Prague. The composition and careful proportional balance reflect the growing emphasis on typographic order and clarity within Czech printing culture.

 

T. Gleitsmann, Drážďany promotional advertisement for a Dresden-based manufacturer of printing inks and graphic colour materials. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 2, 1909. The dark paper stock, metallic framing, and minimal ornamental treatment show a shift away from Art Nouveau decoration toward a cleaner early modern style.

 

Fr. Horáček a M. Triburůžek business stationery and invoice specimens for a Prague glass manufacturer and supplier. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 2, 1909. Designed by Methoděj Kaláb and printed at the Politika printing works in Prague. The compositions use strict framing, dotted borders, and a monogram-like central device, demonstrating a more geometric commercial modernism.

 

Krásná kniha: její technická úprava promotional advertisement for a publication on the technical preparation and design of fine books. Published as a supplement to Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 7, 1909. Designed by Karel Dyrink and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague. The design combines medieval-inspired initials and ornamental framing.

 

Veškerému členstvu spolku Typografia notice issued to members of the Typografia association in Prague concerning membership subscriptions and regulations, dated July 1909. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 7, 1909. Designed by Method Kaláb and printed by Albert Maršíček in Prague. The composition uses strong linear divisions and repeated ornamental panels.

 

Ex libris reproductions from Technické kursy grafické by F. J. Havelka, published in Prague during 1909. Featured in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 7, 1909. The ex libris designs combine expressive illustration with decorative typography and woodcut-inspired linear treatment, reflecting the popularity of bookplate design within Central European Art Nouveau graphics.

 

Rudolfinum concert programme for a performance by the Prague singing society Malát and an academic orchestra, held on Saturday 9 October 1909. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 10, 1909. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed at the Politika printing works in Prague. The composition uses ornament, symmetrical framing, and classical typographic hierarchy, demonstrating increasingly ordered and architectural qualities of typographic design during the period.

 

Spolek Rozvoj v Pardubicích and Zahradní zábavu event posters and programme layouts for social and cultural gatherings in Pardubice and Libní, dated August 1909. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 7, 1909. Designed by A. Chvály and printed at the Politika printing works in Prague. The narrow vertical compositions combine geometric framing devices with ornament and lettering.

 

Máte dobrý tisk? promotional typographic advertisements for the Prague printing firm Novotný a Příhoda in Královské Vinohrady. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, 1909. The compositions feature highly ornamental spiral motifs and bold hand-lettered typography enclosed within oval frames, reflecting expressive decorative tendencies of Czech advertising design.

 

Knihtiskaři Novotný a Příhoda invoice and accounting form for the Prague printing firm in Královské Vinohrady. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, 1909. Designed by M. Novotný and printed by the firm itself. The decorative green ornamental borders and flowing script typography demonstrate how Art Nouveau visual language was used in practical commercial stationery and bookkeeping material.

 

Crikvenice promotional graphic for the Croatian coastal spa resort and climatic health destination of Crikvenica. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, 1909. Designed by M. Novotný and printed by Novotný a Příhoda in Královské Vinohrady. The hanging ornamental motif and linear decoration show simplified geometric structure and remind of the later Art Deco stylisation.

 

Jos. Neff v Praze and Rudolf Houdek v Praze commercial advertisements for Prague-based suppliers of terracotta goods, curtains, ribbons, and carpets. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 11, 1909. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by Fr. Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague. Both designs use repeated spiral ornament and geometric framing, illustrating a refined decorative style of Czech commercial typography.

 

Antonína Reise announcement and promotional circular for a newly established printing house and publishing operation in Prague, located in Královské Vyšehrad. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 11, 1909. Designed by Jaroslav Motyčka and printed by the Antonín Reise printing works. The design combines ornamental framing with flowing calligraphic text, demonstrating a refined balance between Art Nouveau and functional commercial typography.

 

Naše Slovensko stationery and correspondence templates for the Slovak review Naše Slovensko, published in Prague-Královské Vyšehrad. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 10, 1909. Designed by Jaroslav Motyčka and printed by Antonín Reise. The compositions use a folk-inspired geometric ornament and modular framing.

 

Akcidenční sazeč promotional poster advertising the publication Krásná kniha. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 10, 1909. Designed by Karel Dyrink and printed by J. Vlk at the Politika printing works in Prague.

 

Přátelský večírek spolku Svornost programme and invitation designs for a social evening held at Žofín on 9 October 1909. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 10, 1909. Designed and executed by Methoděj Kaláb and printed by Albert Maršíček in Prague. The layouts use repeated ornamental modules and grid-based structures.

 

Deutscher Buchdrucker Kalender cover and calendar page specimens reproduced from German printing material associated with Ludwig Rexhäuser in Leipzig. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 10, 1909 in relation to the technical graphic courses of F. J. Havelka. The examples demonstrate an influence of German Jugendstil typography.

 

Havlena confectionery advertisement and První ples dance invitation for an anniversary ball in Brno, dated 2 February 1910. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 10, 1909. Designed by Matěj Zeman and printed at the Politika printing works in Prague. Both compositions use vertical structures, ornament, and layouts typical of Czech Secession commercial ephemera.

 

XXVII. Zahradní slavnost České besedy v Žatci poster design for a garden festival held on 4 July 1909. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, 1909. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed at the Politika printing works in Prague. The design uses detailed ornamental borders and stylised framing devices inspired by Art Nouveau decorative systems.

 

Přátelský večírek invitation for a social evening organised by the Smíchov branch of the Typografia association, dated 13 March 1909. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 1, 1909. Designed and executed by Method Kaláb and printed by J. Hoffmann in Prague. The composition features strong geometric divisions and stylised ornament panels.

 

Rozmar and Klid smrti book cover designs for Czech literary publications. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 1, 1909. Designed and typeset by Karel Šifner and printed by Ant. Hoffmann in Prague. The covers employ simplified geometric decoration, minimal ornament, and bold lettering arrangements.

 

Elitní vínek and Šibřinky Besedy Jaro dance and masquerade invitations dated February and January 1909. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 1, 1909. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by the Politika printing works in Prague. The compositions combine ornamental framing, and stylised illustration. Decorative Czech print design before a transition toward early modernist simplification.

 

Maškarní vínek and IV. Masopustní večírek invitation designs for carnival and masquerade evenings held in Prague and Nusle during February 1909. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 1, 1909. Designed and executed by M. Bureš and printed by Albert Maršíček in Prague. These compositions combine geometric framing with restrained ornament and flat colour panels.

 

Ladislav Bouška commercial invoice and stationery design for a furniture and carpentry business in Pardubice. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 11, 1909. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by Fr. Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague. The design employs Uses  accounting borders and stylised floral corner motifs.

 

Slévárna písem Česká akciová společnost v Praze promotional cover or specimen design for the Czech type foundry. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 11, 1909. The composition combines decorative geometric patterning with an industrial illustration of a craftsman operating printing machinery.

 

Odražení čepele book spread and typographic layout specimen. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 11, 1909. Designed and executed by Methoděj Kaláb and printed by Albert Maršíček in Prague. The layout has a refined page architecture, decorative paragraph initials, and use of green ornamentation.

 

Josef Toman i spol. memorandum and business stationery design for a company based in Poděbrady. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 5, 1909. Designed by Karel Šifner and printed at the Politika printing works in Prague.

 

Zoha and Ant. Beyr commercial advertising designs for interior decoration and upholstery businesses in Královské Vinohrady. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 10, 1909. Designed by Alois Chvála and printed by J. Nosek and Příhoda in Prague. The examples use geometric ornament and carefully proportioned lettering structures characteristic of Czech Secession commercial ephemera.

 

Koncert dělnického zpěváckého sdružení v Lounech programme and concert invitation dated 20 May 1909. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 4, 1909. Designed by Karel Kubeš and printed at the Th. Venty printing works in Prague. The design uses delicate floral ornament and musical symbolism.

 

Účastníkům studijní cesty českých typografů do Německa informational circular produced for Czech typographers undertaking a study trip to Germany. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 4, 1909. Designed and executed by Methoděj Kaláb and printed by Albert Maršíček in Prague. The design reflects the admiration Czech printers held for technical and typographic detail.

 

Veleslavín, společnost přátel krásné knihy české v Praze membership certificate and Zábavný večírek invitation for a clerical workers’ association evening held on 13 March 1909. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 4, 1909. Designed by Karel Dyrink and printed by J. Zapotil at the Politika printing works. The compositions combine ornamental initials, framing, and simplified typographic organisation.

 

Pamětní listina commemorative certificate for the twentieth anniversary of the civic association Ruch in Benešov, dated 1889–1909. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 4, 1909. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by Fr. Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague. The design has structured composition and repeated ornamental forms.

 

Programme and menu design produced for the III. International Congress of Chambers of Commerce in Prague, dated September 1908. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 4, 1909. Printed by J. Jenšek at the Politika printing works in Prague. The work demonstrates how Czech typographers adapted Art Nouveau ornament into delicate typographic compositions.

 

Domácí večírek invitation for the Besedy Havlíček association in Plzeň and Ples Svazu českých dílovedoucích v Praze dance programme. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 1, 1909. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works.

 

Decorative title page for Typografia: odborný list knihtiskařů marking the twentieth year of publication of the Czech typographic journal. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 1, 1909. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by Fr. Málek in Prague. The composition combines ornamental panels with carefully structured typography, presenting the journal itself as a showcase of contemporary Czech printing and design standards.

 

Masopustní merendu carnival programme and Zahradnický ples invitation designs for social and dance events held in Prague during March 1909. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 3, 1909. Designed by M. Bureš and printed by Politika in Prague. The layouts integrate ornament, framing, and small figurative illustrations, revealing the continued popularity of decorative design within Czech graphic design.

 

III. Den smíchovských typografů na Plzence event poster and programme for a typographers’ gathering organised by the Smíchov branch of the Typografia association. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 6, 1909. Designed by Methoděj Kaláb and printed by Albert Maršíček in Prague. The poster uses repeated geometric motifs arranged within a strict grid.

 

Commercial stationery and invoice designs for Bedřich Houžvička v Dobrovici, a clockmaking and mechanical business established in 1875. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 6, 1909. Designed by Emanuel Petlan and printed by Jan Vojtíšek at the Hedja & Zbroj printing works in Mladá Boleslav.

 

Book cover or memorial print titled Memento by Adolf Kvapil, published by the Neruda association and printed at the Workers’ Printing House in Prague-II during 1909. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 6, 1909. Designed by Methoděj Kaláb. The work combines restrained black linear geometry with a vivid floral illustration.

 

Commercial card and business stationery designs for M. Trnobranský and representative Rudolf Valášek, associated with a paint factory in Kralupy. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 5, 1909. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at Politika in Prague. The designs feature repeating geometric ornament.

 

Invoice and accounting sheet for the Dělnická knihtiskárna a nakladatelství v Praze, Myslíkova Street. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 5, 1909. Designed and executed by Methoděj Kaláb and printed by Albert Maršíček in Prague. The design transforms ordinary business stationery into a sophisticated typographic composition.

 

Program reprezentačního večera umělecké besedy ve Slaném programme cover and internal page for an artistic society evening featuring works by composers including Dvořák and Gounod. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 5, 1909. Designed by Alois Chvála and printed by Josef Vlk in Slaný.

 

Book cover design for Léto (“Summer”), a collection of poetry and prose gathered from mountain and rural life by Jaroslav Nedbal and Bohuš Hvořanský. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 5, 1909. Designed by Alois Chvála and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague. The composition uses geometric framing with repeated triangular ornament and vertical striped elements.

 

Cover proposal for Povídky verší a prosou by E. Duchaň, published by the Moderna society and printed by V. Hrubýin Třebová. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 3, 1909. Designed by Otokar Císař. The layout is highly structured, built from modular rectangular divisions.

 

Commercial advertisement cards for Karel Strnad, a florist in Prague, and Jan Dejl, a cabinetmaker and furniture manufacturer. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 3, 1909. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at Politika in Prague. Both works show an adaptation of modern geometric organisation to small commercial print.

 

Programme and invitation designs for commemorative and social events including the 20th anniversary celebration of the Ruch association in Choceň and a Zábavný večírek organised by a readers’ society in Pardubice. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 3, 1909. Designed by Methoděj Kaláb and printed by Politika in Prague. The use of repetitive floral borders and compartmentalised layouts show a growing influence of structured design within Czech applied graphics.

 

Programme design for an Umělecký večírek organised by the Hálek association in Prague to celebrate its tenth anniversary, dated March 1909. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 3, 1909. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at Politika in Prague. The cover has delicate floral illustration with a linear framework, reflecting a merging of decorative Art Nouveau with typographic precition.

 

Engagement and marriage announcement cards for Anna Tichých and Josef Srp, and Václav Novák and Věnceslava Kratochvílová. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 3, 1909. Designed and typeset by Karel Šifner and printed by Jan Bárta in Prague. These refined social announcements use garlands, thin borders, and a structured typographic hierachy.

 

New Year greeting card produced for the editorial administration of Typografie. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 12, 1909. Designed by Karel Šifner and printed by Albert Maršíček in Prague. The compact square composition uses repeating geometric corner ornaments for decoration. This scanned artefacts shows how festive ephemera became a vehicle for experimenting with modern decorative typography.

 

Wine advertisement and carnival invitation designs including a promotional notice for the Prague wine merchant Jan Dubský and a Masopustní věneček invitation organised by the Litografická Beseda association in February 1910. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 12, 1909. Designed by Karel Dyrýnka and printed by A. Mráz at Politika in Prague. These works use expressive illustrative elements while maintaining the geometric framing systems used in the other examples I have scanned.

 

Letterhead and envelope designs for Pražská Lidová Revue. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 10, 1909. Designed by Otto Kysela and printed by František Málek at Politika in Prague.

 

Promotional broadside for the Pěvecký odbor spolku Typografia v Praze. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 9, 1909. Designed by Rudolf Ondráček and printed by Josef Vlk in Prague. The richly coloured composition combines ornamental floral panels with strong typographic hierarchy..

 

Wine list design for the Hotel U Koruny in Český Krumlov. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 9, 1909. Designed and executed by Karel Šifner and printed by Bohumil Horděk in Prague. The composition combines delicate grapevine ornament and an illustrated portrait.

 

Book cover proposals for Zo d’Axa: Z Mazasu do Jerusalema and Bohdan Kaminský: Pohádky. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 9, 1909. Designed by Methoděj Kaláb and printed by Albert Maršíček in Prague. Both covers reduce ornament compared to other scanned examples from 1909 to minimal framing device and sparse symbolic motifs.

 

Commercial stationery and advertisement designs for K. Holský, an artistic printing works in Jičín, and Roman & Valson, watch suppliers in Kolín. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 9, 1909. Designed by Matěj Zeman and printed by František Málek at Politika in Prague. These examples combine strong typographic structure with small illustrative panels and decorative borders.

 

Programme sheet for a 1909 performance of Carmen presented by the Typografia association at the Municipal Theatre of Královské Vinohrady in Prague. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 9, 1909. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by Josef Vlk at Politika in Prague.

 

Invitation for a Maškarní Vínek (masked carnival dance) organised by the workers’ gymnastic association “Marx” in Žižkov. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 12, 1909. Designed by Jarka Motyčka and printed by Antonín Reiss at Královské Vinohrady. The composition combines decorative illustration with text in rectangle compartments..

 

New Year greeting card designs for a Prague printing house. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 12, 1909. Designed by Methoděj Kaláb and printed by Jaroslav Bošek in Prague.

 

Invitation and dance programme designs for the Zástěrkový Vínek organised by the Svornost association in Prague, dated January 1910. Published in Typografia, Vol. XX, Issue 10, 1909. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at Politika in Prague.

title.rendered: Advertising Design for Pražská Lidová Revue Magazine

content.rendered:
Typografia was a Czech typography and printing journal first published in Prague in 1888. I have collected over 400 issues and continue to source the remaining missing volumes for the archive. Each issue included finely printed supplementary sheets featuring decorative commercial printing specimens, business stationery, advertisements, and typographic layouts, offering valuable examples of contemporary Czech typography and commercial printing practice.

I have scanned in at high-resolution fourty of the sample sheets from the eighteenth volume in 1907.

 

Art Nouveau advertisement and commercial designs for Jan Hryzal of Prague and the printing works of Václav Staroch in Žižkov. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 7, 1907. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by Adolf Dvořák at the Politika printing works in Prague. The restrained compositions and simplified geometric ornament reflect the decorative Art Nouveau and functional commercial typography.

 

Invitation and programme designs for Czech cultural and educational associations, including a humorous evening organised by Spolek Flora and a recitation evening organised by the Svatopluk Čech educational association in Roztoky, dated August 1907. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 7, 1907. Designed by M. Bureš and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague. The designs combine Secession style framing with expressive illustrative portrait motifs.

 

Geometric programme designs for the fortieth anniversary celebrations of Spolek Tyl in Tábor, dated 28 July 1907. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 7, 1907. Designed by Method Kaláb and printed by Jaroslav Hoffmann at the printing works of Otakar Zdeněk in Prague.

 

Decorative commercial letterheads and stationery designs for Karel Návratník of Smíchov, Jos. Morávek & Co. of Prague-Libeň, and the Havel Maděra pharmacy and wine business in Královské Vinohrady. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 7, 1907. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague. These examples combine geometric framing with ornamental motifs, illustrating Czech commercial typography and design during the Secession era.

 

Symbolist book cover design for Kamil Bílý’s V Olsinách (In the Alder Groves), published by the Orion publishing cooperative in Uherské Hradiště. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 7, 1907. Designed by K. Karás and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague. This example has a gradient style background and is less retrained in backgraound colour than the other examples I have scanned.

 

Reprezentační Věneček dance programme and event stationery for the Beseda Tyl association in Prague, dated 2 February 1907. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 6, 1907. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed at the Politika printing works in Prague. The composition uses repeated circular ornamental elements and framing, demonstrating the refined geometric tendencies emerging within late Czech Secession typography.

 

Minimal linear letterhead and advertisement designs for Josef Vlčík of Beroun, specialising in painting, decorating, and gilding. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 6, 1907. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by Adolf Dvořák at the Politika printing works in Prague. The geometric framing and restrained ornament anticipate later modernist approaches to corporate stationery and applied typography.

 

Geometric commercial typography for the Apollo soap and starch factory in Písek and M. Kosík timber works in Prague. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 6, 1907. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague. The bold borders and repetitive angular motifs have an abstract and architectonic form.

 

II. Grafický Večer promotional programme for the Typografia Association in Prague, 1907. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 6, 1907. Designed by Otokar Císař and lithographed by Josef Šercl at the Politika printing works in Prague. The structured composition, pastel palette, and hanging decorative motifs reflect the influence of the Viennese and Czech Art Nouveau design.

 

Art Nouveau wine advertisement for Ceres fruit wine and menu design for Hotel Paříž, Prague, dated 24 May 1907. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 6, 1907. Designed and executed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek. The elegant framing and delicate ornamental curves demonstrate the refinement of Czech commercial print design during the later Secession period.

 

Decorative commercial typography and stationery designs for the jewellery and silverware firm Fr. J. Herman, operating in Plzeň, Prague, and Turnov. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 5, 1907. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed at the Politika printing works in Prague. The work uses stylised floral motifs and line structures, balancing ornament with typographic organisation.

 

Havraní Stříbro advertising placard for a stove and metal paint product distributed by Rudolf Rez of Mladá Boleslav. Produced as part of the graphic course organised by the Municipal Industrial Museum in Hradec Králové and published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 5, 1907. Designed by A. Moravec. The raven silhouette and simplified layout demonstrate bold pictorial advertising and reduction in advertising.

 

Certificate design for the Municipal Typographic Course organised by the Municipal Industrial Museum in Hradec Králové, 1907. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 5, 1907. Designed by Otokar Císař and executed by Antonín J. Tymeš. The composition combines geometric ornament with Secession detailing, reflecting the growing professionalisation of typographic education in the early twentieth century.

 

Typographic title pages produced during the graphic course organised by the Municipal Industrial Museum in Hradec Králové, 1907. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 5, 1907. The examples, including works by V. Brunát and J. Kotek, demonstrate simplified decorative structure within Czech book design education.

 

Minimal geometric typography for industrial pattern books and society publications, including designs for locksmith J. Míša and the Machar Society of Smíchov. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 5, 1907. Designed by Alois Stork and printed at the Politika printing works in Prague. The reduction of ornament and proportion, spacing, and framing are a great eaxmaple of early modernist Czech design.

 

Commercial advertisement layouts for Karel Heveroch and the painting and varnishing company Fr. Hermann of Prague. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 8, 1907. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague. The work balances geometric framing with subtle ornamental detailing.

 

Decorative commercial letterheads for B. Fr. Zrnka and the sculptural and masonry firm Karel Vávroch & Co. of Prague. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 12, 1907. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague. The highly structured layouts and repeated geometric border systems reveal an increasingly modern approach to business stationery design.

 

Art Nouveau hotel menu designs for Jan Kohout and Hotel Čechie in Liberec, 1907. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 12, 1907. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague. The vine ornamentation and softened pastel palette demonstrate the continued influence of floral Secession motifs within print design.

 

Geometric Art Nouveau trade catalogue and paint sample designs for Prague manufacturers Podubský & Co. and M. Hájek. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 12, 1907. Designed by Karel Šifnera and printed by František Pštrosský at the Th. Unert printing establishment in Prague. The designs combine ornament with strongly structured vertical compositions.

 

Statute cover design for the Smetana Society and commercial advertisement layout for A. Vlach of Prague. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 12, 1907. Designed by M. Kalába and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague.

 

Catalogue and advertisement layouts for F. Topič, publisher and manufacturer of artistic reproductions in Prague, Budějovice, Plzeň, and Olomouc. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 11, 1907. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed at the Politika printing works in Prague.

 

Concert programme design for Hudební Večer organised by the educational society Bendl in Prague, 1907. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 11, 1907. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague. The architectural framing, geometric ornament, and finely balanced typographic hierarchy create a sophisticated example of Czech design.

 

Evening programme design and cover for the Český Zahradnický Almanach (Czech Gardening Almanac), 1907. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 11, 1907. Designed by M. Bureš and printed by A. Maršíček at the Dělnická printing works. The stylised floral ornament, decorative panels, and symbolic female illustration demonstrate the continued influence of Czech Secession illustration in applied print design.

 

Price list and bookbinding cover designs for Karhan & Rybař of Prague and the bookbinder R. Melan. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 11, 1907. Designed by K. Šifnera and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague.

 

Decorative calendar design for the Politika printing and publishing house for the year 1908. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 11, 1907. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague. The symmetrical ornamental framework, stylised grape motifs, and delicate linear detailing combine commercial design with refined Art Nouveau decorative design.

 

Cover design for Moderní Tisky, published by the Typografia Association in Prague, 1907. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 10, 1907. Designed by J. Mrkvička and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works.

 

Art Nouveau commercial stationery designs for Union, the First Prague Decorative Glassworks, and jeweller K. Melan of Prague. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 11, 1907. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed at the Politika printing works in Prague.

 

Commercial label and packaging designs for F. Rak mineral water products and Helios shoe polish paste. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 10, 1907. Designed by R. Karas and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague.

 

Promotional design for the XXI Český Typografický Almanach for the year 1908. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 10, 1907. Designed by M. Bureš and printed by A. Maršíček at the Dělnická printing works. The composition combines stylised female portraiture with geometric framing.

 

Commercial stationery and event invitation designs by Method Kaláb, including an advertisement for Fr. Materna and invitations for Czech cultural associations and public events in 1907. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 9, 1907. Printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague.

 

Menu design and evening programme invitation for the Osvěta Society. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 9, 1907. Designed by Method Kaláb and printed by Jaroslav Hoffmann at the printing works of Otakar Janáček in Prague. The stylised birds, classical framing devices, and flattened decorative illustration demonstrate the persistence of symbolic Art Nouveau imagery within Czech design.

 

Geometric commercial typography designs for the financial company Securitas and the statutes publication of the Glove Workers’ Association of Prague and surrounding areas. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 9, 1907. Designed by Method Kaláb and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works.

 

Commercial advertising designs for the steelworks company Ocelárny D. Grosse of Polish Ostrava and a Kodak promotional design dated 1907. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 9, 1907. Designed by Method Kaláb and printed by Jaroslav Hoffmann at the printing works of Otakar Janáček in Prague.

 

Commercial advertisement for the artistic gardening business of J. Soukupa alongside an invitation design for the Osvěta Society dance evening, 1907. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 9. Designed by Method Kaláb and printed by Albert Maršíček at the Dělnická printing works in Prague. Both designs combine delicate ornamental framing with simplified geometric structure.

 

Programme design for the celebration of the Union of Industrial Workers of Prague-Libeň, held at Žofín in 1907. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 8, 1907. Designed by Method Kaláb and printed by Jaroslav Hoffmann at the printing house of Otakar Janáček in Prague. The linear construction and repeated circular mechanical motifs suggest an industrial interpretation of Czech decorative modernism.

 

Programme and invitation designs for the educational association Marx in Prague-VI, 1907. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 8, 1907. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by Adolf Dvořák at the Politika printing works in Prague. The strict symmetry, vertical framing and restrained decorative motifs demonstrate a different interpretation of Art Nouveau.

 

Letterhead competition designs for the Municipal Industrial Museum in Hradec Králové. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 8, 1907. Printed by B. Petřina in Hradec Králové. The geometric borders, motifs, and reduced ornamental language reflect the growing influence of structural modernity within Czech commercial typography.

 

Concert programme design for the educational association Vítkov held at the Rudolfinum, Prague, 1907. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 8, 1907. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works. The composition combines stylised floral illustration, decorative framing, and  geometry characteristic of Czech Art Nouveau print design.

 

Advertising design for Pražská Lidová Revue, an educational and cultural magazine published in Prague. Published in Typografia, Vol. XVIII, Issue 8, 1907. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works. The geometric lettering, restrained ornament, and flat colour planes demonstrate the transition from Czech Secession design toward a more simplified commercial style of typography.

 

Typografia documented Czech commercial printing for over 100 years. These examples show the decorative style of Art Nouveau and the structural clarity that would define early modernism. Designers like Otokar Císař, Method Kaláb, Mořic Novotný and Karel Šifnera worked across many of the examples applying Secessionist ornament to the everyday demands of commercial print. The archive holds over 400 issues of Typografia spanning more than a century of Czech printing history, and further articles will be added as scanning continues.

Find out more about early Czech typography and print culture in the archive. Read 50 examples of Czech Typography from 1908 and explore the Art Nouveau and Jugendstil and New Typography movements. title.rendered: Catalogue cover design for a pipe and cement goods factory. Designed by Otokar Císař

content.rendered:
Typografia is a Czech typography and printing journal and was first released in 1888 in Prague. I have collected over 400 issues and continue to source the missing volumes for the archive. Each issues featured a selection of fine printed supplements of decorative commercial printing specimens, business stationery, advertisements, and typographic layouts, each a fine example of contemporary Czech typography and commercial printing practice. I have scanned in at high-resolution, fifty of the sample sheets from the nineteenth volume, published in 1908.

Invitation card and dance programme designs for the Czech Lawyers’ Association ball at Žofín, Prague, 1909. Published as a supplement to Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 12, 1908. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing house in Prague. The geometric ornament and restrained colour palette reflect a transition from Art Nouveau towards early modern decorative typography.

 

Commercial stationery and advertising designs for Hejda & Zbroj printing works and Jaroslav Draský furniture warehouse in Mladá Boleslav. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 12, 1908. Designed by Emil Petlan and printed by J. Plass. These designs combine lettering and modular ornament.

 

New Year greeting card designs for the year, 1909 reproduced in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 12, 1908. The upper card was produced for the Politika printing house in Prague, while the lower design advertises the workshop of František Brůna in Pardubice.

 

Title page for Typografia, Vol. XIX, 1908 designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek in Prague, 1908. The composition combines vertical ornament with restrained typography, reflecting the influence of the Viennese Secession.

 

Letterhead and correspondence card designs for the advertising office of F. Mázel in Královské Vinohrady, Prague. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 10, 1908. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed at the Politika printing works. The ornamental borders and floral motifs show the influence of Art Nouveau typography in Czech commercial graphics.

 

Advertising design for the Politika printing house in Prague, reproduced in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 11, 1908. Designed by St. Musil and printed by František Málek. The piece uses more colour than previous examples, especially in the ornamental border.

 

Invitation and programme designs for a theatre society evening event held at Hotel Merkur, 1908. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 11, 1908. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek in Prague. The balanced composition and stylised floral ornament demonstrate the influence of Viennese and Czech Secessionist decorative graphics.

 

Commercial letterhead and invoice designs for Czech businesses including R. Drvotka a Synové, František Gottschalk and Miroslav Karásek. Published in Typografie, Vol. XIX, Issue 11, 1908. Designed by Karel Šifner and printed by Antonín Hofmann in Prague. The designs use modular geometry, ornament and reduced colour palettes associated with early twentieth-century Czech decorative typography.

 

Commercial advertising and correspondence card designs for textile and furniture manufacturers, published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 11, 1908. Designed and printed by Method Kaláb and Otakar Janáček in Prague. Simplified organic ornament and one-colour.

 

Advertising design for the printing workshop of Otakar Janáček, Prague, published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 12, 1908. Designed by Method Kaláb and printed by Otakar Janáček. The composition combines geometric framing, stylised ornament and bold lettering showing commercial typography in 1908.

 

Cover design for the sixth catalogue of books published by the educational association Neruda in Prague, 1908. Published as a supplement to Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 8, 1908. Designed by Method Kaláb and printed at the Politika printing house in Prague. Bold block lettering and repetitive vertical geometry show modernist approaches to typographic composition.

 

Invitation design for a social evening organised by the cycling club “Ruch” in Královské Vinohrady, Prague. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 7, 1908. Designed by Jaroslav Motyčka and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works. The floral wreath motifs and elongated vertical structure reflect Czech Art Nouveau.

 

Commercial advertising designs for Hugo Carmine, supplier of printing machinery and graphic materials with offices in Prague, Vienna and Budapest. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 8, 1908. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek in Prague. The compositions combine geometric ornament, bold typography and contrasting colour palettes.

 

Hotel Union advertising design for hotelier Jan Blaho, published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 10, 1908. Designed by Karel Šifner and printed at the Politika printing house in Prague. The composition features restrained geometric framing and stylised ornament influenced by Viennese Secession.

 

Cover design for Nové Ukázky Tisků (“New Printing Specimens”), Vol. XIX, designed by Method Kaláb and printed by Jaroslav Hofmann at the Otakar Janáček printing works in Prague.

 

Wine merchant advertisement for Václav Karás in Prague, published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 10, 1908. Designed by František Hapala and printed by Jaroslav Procházka at the Edvard Lesching printing house in Prague. Decorative borders and linear ornament merge Art Nouveau influences with structured typographic layout.

 

Book cover design for Maryša by K. Picka, published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 9, 1908. Designed by Mořic Novotný and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague. This design has a reduced ornament compared to the others and a muted colour palette.

 

Letterhead and correspondence card designs for Dr. Ladislav Radimský’s milling and timber business in Kolín. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 9, 1910. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek in Prague. A grwat example of Viennese Secession typography in use on Czech commercial stationery.

 

Advertising poster for a dairy and butter supplier, published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 9, 1908. Designed by St. Musil and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing house in Prague. The simplified landscape illustration and flat illustration is a contrast to the other examples and leans more towards the advertising graphics that were designed in Germany in the 1900s.

 

Commercial stationery and advertising designs for Václav Kindl, supplier of printing machinery and graphic materials in Prague. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 8, 1908. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works.

 

Commercial stationery and advertising designs for Václav Kindl, supplier of printing machinery and graphic materials in Prague. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 7, 1908. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works. The designs combines intricate ornamental borders, almost like the work of William Morris.

 

Book cover proposal for Jan Neruda: Jeho Spisy a Životopis (“His Writings and Biography”), published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 7, 1908. Designed by Method Kaláb and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing house in Prague. The repetition and structured typography anticipate later modernist book design developments.

 

Advertising design for the František Křižík electrotechnical factory in Prague-Karlín, founded in 1884. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 5, 1908. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed at the Politika printing works in Prague. The composition combines electrical symbolism, geometric framing and decorative stripes, it reminds me of the work for AEG designed by Peter Behrens.

 

Commercial identity and advertising layouts for goldsmith and decorative arts workshop Josef Nový of Prague. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 6, 1908. Designed by Mořic Novotný and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works.

 

Advertising design for the watch manufacturer F. Nedoma of Prague, published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 6, 1908. Designed by Alois Chvály and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing house. This narrow composition and simplified clock motif merge decorative Art Nouveau characteristics into a modern geometric structure.

 

Decorative typographic design for Přilétlo k nám jaro zdaleka (“Spring Flew to Us from Afar”), a ballad by Antonín Jahný. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 6, 1908. Designed by Mořic Novotný and printed by František Málek in Prague. The design features floral forms and restrained geometric arrangement.

 

Poster and exhibition announcement for an exhibition of enamel products by the F. Sommerschuh factory at the Prague Exchange building, held from 15 May to 31 July 1908. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 6, 1908. Designed by Mořic Novotný and printed by Jindřich Zapotil at the Politika printing works. The design uses simplified geometry and tiled ornament influenced by the Viennese Secession movement.

 

Commercial printing and exhibition invitation designs for B. Fr. Zrnka of Prague, specialists in printing, lithography and bookbinding. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 7, 1908. Designed by Karel Dyrinka and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing house.

 

Letterhead and commercial stationery designs for Jan Frinta of Libeň, Th. Venta of Prague, and Václav Ventruba of Opava. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 5, 1908. Designed by Karel Šifner and printed at the Politika printing works in Prague. The designs use simplified ornamental motifs and geometric framing.

 

Invoice and accounting form design for the carpenter Adolf Chittussi of Prague II, Vodíčkova Street. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 5, 1908. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed at the Politika printing house in Prague. Decorative woodworking symbols and carefully structured grids merge functional commercial design with Secessionist ornament.

 

Cover design for Illustrovaný Vzorník Koberců (“Illustrated Pattern Book of Carpets”), issued by the Zemský Spolek Textilníků in Prague and compiled by Professor František Staněk. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 4, 1908. Designed by Stanislav Musila and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works.

 

Commercial stationery and advertising layouts for Václav Kindl of Prague, specialist supplier to the printing and bookbinding trades. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 4, 1908. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing house. The design uses decorative Secessionist motifs with clear typographic structure and spacing.

 

Examples of graphic work produced for the newly founded Spolek Bibliophilů (“Society of Bibliophiles”) in Prague. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 4, 1908. Designed by Karel Dyrynk and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works. The invitations show the interest in fine printing, book arts, and private press in early Czech design culture.

 

Decorative title and announcement designs including Coloured Etchings by Vojtěch Preissig and a wedding announcement for Vlasta Vaňousů and Jindřich Juřena. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 5, 1908. The design accompanied an article on his typography and demonstrates his distinctive combination of stylised lettering and ornamental forms.

 

Programme and invitation designs for the Umělecká Akademie Besedy Tyl in Plzeň, commemorating the centenary of Josef Kajetán Tyl in March 1908. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 2, 1908. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works.

 

Poster and informational leaflet designs for an exhibition of student work from typographic courses organised by the Technological Industrial Museum in Prague. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 2, 1908. Designed and printed by František Málek. The simplified printing press illustration and structured page composition demonstrate the growing interest in modern commercial typography and graphic education.

 

Advertising designs for the insert advertising office of F. Mázel and the Prague flower wholesaler A. Herfurth. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 3 1908. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works. The decorative floral elements and geometric style show the merging of commercial advertising with Art Nouveau ornamentation.

 

Programme and invitation designs for an Umělecká Akademie cultural event organised in Smíchov, Prague, during March 1908. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 3, 1908. Designed by Arnold František Randák and printed by Albert Maršík in Prague. The ornamental hanging garlands, fountain imagery and stylised details demonstrate the continued influence of Secessionist decorative graphics in Czech design.

 

Commercial catalogue and wine price-list designs for Emil Simon and C. Mik of Prague. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 3, 1908. Designed by Stanislav Musila and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing house. The reduced geometric structure and stylised elements show the transition from ornamental Art Nouveau towards a more simplified decorative modernism.

 

Catalogue cover design for the pipe and cement goods factory of R. Bitner in České Budějovice. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 4, 1908. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works.

 

Programme and invitation designs for artistic evenings organised by the Typografia association in Prague during March 1908. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 1, 1908. The left design was created by Antonín Pospíšil, while the right was designed by A. Štorch. Both works demonstrate the restrained geometry and stylised ornament characteristic of Czech Secession typography.

 

Invitation and programme designs for a charitable evening event organised by the educational society Osvěta in Smíchov, Prague, March 1908. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 1, 1908. Designed and printed by M. Bureš at the Albert Maršík printing house in Prague. The layout, decorative motifs, and carefully balanced typography reflect the influence of Viennese Secession design on Czech printed ephemera.

 

Decorative greeting and wedding announcement cards including a marriage announcement for Olga Suchá and Vojtěch Modráček and a New Year greeting designed for the bookseller Karel Záhorský. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 1, 1908. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works in Prague.

 

Commercial typographic layouts for the printing house of F. Milota in České Budějovice and the Prague bookbinding workshop of Fr. Hala. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 2, 1908. Designed by A. Štorch and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works.

 

Examples of commercial advertising typography for Karel Nápravník, Ferdinand Wilhelm, and the Velvety Goods Factory in Střešovice. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 2, 1908. Designed by Karel Šimera and printed by František Pštrossmý in Prague.

 

Menu and banquet programme designs created for celebratory events held in Prague during January 1908, including a menu for Hotel Metropol. Published in Typografia, Vol. XIX, Issue 2, 1908. Designed by Otokar Císař and printed by František Málek at the Politika printing works.

 

Typografia documented Czech commercial printing for over 100 years. These examples show the decorative style of Art Nouveau and the structural clarity that would define early modernism. Designers like Otokar Císař, Method Kaláb, and Mořic Novotný worked across many of the examples applying Secessionist ornament to the everyday demands of commercial print. The archive holds over 400 issues of Typografia spanning more than a century of Czech printing history, and further articles will be added as scanning continues.

Find out more about early Czech typography and print culture in the archive. title.rendered: The work of the Steglitz Workshop. 1900 – Graphic Design History

content.rendered:
This is the first of a series of articles focusing on graphic design year by year, which I intend to go from 1900-2000.The series will be illustrated with artefacts from the archive, scanned inners (in which I don’t currently have any original material) and relevant quotes and reference for further reading. I will also be revisiting this series from time-to-time as I uncover more content and add further artefacts to the archive. The series will also help me find gaps in the archive, in which I feel documentation isn’t on the website, and information and key pieces to be uploaded and purchased as I go.

Although 1900 was the first year I wanted to focus on, the previous few years had seen the emergence of the Art Nouveau movement, which is regarded as one of the first international art movements. It became an international style and had a major influence on the design of books, posters and typeface design. Across Europe its variations of style and terms include Jugendstil, Modernismo, Secession and Stile Floreale.

 

Art Nouveau was in full swing and the German magazine Jugend was promoting the German Art Nouveau movement, as well as the magazines, Typografia and Deutsche Kunst Und Dekoration.

Jugend was first published in 1896 and was founded in Munich by Georg Hirth. It was a weekly magazine and ‘originally intended to showcase German Arts and Crafts, but became famous for showcasing the German version of Art Nouveau instead’. Its covers were influential and with over two thousand issues it showcased a range of artists including Hans Christiansen and Bruno Paul.

 

 

1900 was also the year that Karl Klingspor of the Rudhard Type Foundry in Offenbach commissioned Otto Eckmann to design the Eckmann-Schrift typeface. The typeface reflected the flowing forms and ornamental qualities associated with Parisian and Berlin poster design of the period and became closely associated with German Jugendstil. Combining blackletter-inspired structures with organic, calligraphic curves, Eckmann-Schrift remains one of the defining typefaces of the Art Nouveau era.

Ohno Type’s account of the typeface’s origins captures its significance well:

‘Seeds were planted in 1899 as the masthead for the magazine Die Woche, an illustrated weekly newspaper. Eckmann then translated that lettering into a full typeface, but it seems that type was just a single facet of his many skills. Trained as a painter, Eckmann ditched his purely artistic pursuits later in life to focus on applied design. It’s wonderful to see the influence of a true artist on his type. His eponymous work remains one of the most original and enduring Art Nouveau contributions in type design history.’
Ohno Type – The Process of Eckmannpsych

 

The first major design studio is often considered to have emerged in October 1900 with the formation of the Steglitz Workshop in Steglitz, near Berlin. Founded by Georg Belwe, Fritz Helmuth Ehmcke, and Friedrich Wilhelm Kleukens, the group met while studying at the teaching institute of the Berlin Museum of Decorative Arts, where some had already learned lithographic techniques in the museum’s workshops.

The recently released Eckmann-Schrift from the Rudhard Type Foundry quickly became an influence on the group. The Steglitz artists purchased a set of the typeface and used it in their earliest printed works, initially produced in small editions for friends and acquaintances.

Here are a few examples of their work scanned from Deutsche Kunst Und Dekoration, Vol XIII, Oktober 1903 – Marz 1904

 

 

 

In this same year, Peter Behrens published one of the first books to use a sans serif typeface as running text, Fest des Lebens und der Kunst. This remains highly collectible and a book I would one day love to add to the archive.

In England, the Doves Press was established in Hammersmith, London by T.J. Cobden-Sanderson and Emery Walker, two years after the Kelmscott Press ended. They had a policy that, ‘books should be free from ornament  and owe their design quality to the architectural beauty of the pages’.

Outside of design, 1900, was the year the Eiffel Tower and the Metro celebrated openings at the World Exposition in Paris and the first hamburger, metal-capped bottled coca cola and Hershey’s Chocolate were introduced in America.

 

 

 

 

As this first in the series shows, a lot can happen in just a year,  international magazines, typeface designs, design collectibles and private presses such as the Steglitz Workshop and Doves Press, although there is so much more to research and add. Looking at my collected artefacts today, it becomes possible to trace the transition from nineteenth-century decorative traditions into something far more modern, experimental and international.  I will be continuing to add to these year-by-year articles as I acquire more items and conduct more research.
