Modernist Graphic Design in Britain 1945–1980
Ian McLaren and Tony Pritchard

Chapter two of ‘Modernist Graphic Design in Britain 1945–1980’ focuses attention on the leading design schools of this period. This extract highlights the importance that the Central School of Arts and Crafts played in establishing the connection between design education and the emerging professional practice. An examination of those teaching and studying here during the late 1940s and early 1950s indicates the impact the participants were having on the evolution of what would become the design curriculum in many of the art schools that followed.

 

The Central School of Arts and Crafts

Art and design in Britain owes a great deal to William Johnstone. The son of a modest farmer on the Scottish borders, he came to London via Edinburgh, Paris and California. When appointed to principalship of the Central School of Arts and Crafts (the Central) during the late 1940s, he assembled a remarkable staff team. As a result, because of Johnstone’s enthusiasm and methods, during the immediate post-war period, the Central was without question the most dynamic art school in the country. Its department of Book Production, headed by Jesse Collins, was instrumental in assisting the development of many of the designers who played key roles in the evolution of the discipline, which became known as graphic design. Profiles of several of them are included later in Chapter 3.

 

William Johnstone

In his colourful autobiography, Johnstone describes how in Paris during the 1920s he mixed with such figures as Chagall, Giacommetti, Duchamp, L’Hôte, Poliakoff, Utrillo, and Zadkine.1 When ultimately he came to London he received constant support and encouragement from the Chief Art Inspector for the London County Council (LCC), RR Tomlinson (of whom more later). At the Regent Street Polytechnic (now part of the University of Westminster) Johnstone taught in the Craft School, where he was one of the first to help design cars. To give an idea of the period, he says “there was a growing feeling that, as the motor engine was really different from a horse, the design of a whole car should be different from, say, a hansom cab. It was a transitional period. The fashion was just beginning for the car body to slope away both in the front and at the back, the great idea being to get away as far as possible from the notion of a carriage on wheels”.

Johnstone’s first appointment as a Principal was at Hackney School of Art, which was a centre for evening classes. Here he found Richard Guyatt and Misha Black, both on the staff (of whom more later). He describes “the tremendous rush of students after the war”. This was due to the Ministry of Education having stipulated that places should be found to avoid the “recurrence of the disillusionment after the first World War.” With encouragement from Tomlinson he applied and was appointed to the principalship of Camberwell School of Art (now one of the colleges of the University of the Arts, London). He describes how he was advised that in order to inspire respect from parents he adopted a sober suit, black homburg hat, and carried an umbrella. Amongst the staff was Eric Fraser, who for many decades illustrated the Radio Times, usually in inventive scraper-board. One of the first appointments he made was Victor Pasmore, whom despite his limited qualifications at the time, he classed as having “exquisite taste. Every bit of colour he put together was sensitive”.2 It was here that he first encountered Jesse Collins.

 

 

Johnstone describes how London County Council’s Education Officer’s Department was virtually autonomous from national government. This was strengthened by the fact that the head of the London County Council Education Department, Herbert Morrison, “ruled London as an empire in itself…retaining only a polite link with the Ministry of Education”. He goes on to say “The Chief Art Inspector of the London County Council was superior in intelligence and judgement to his opposite number at the Ministry and would override the Ministry officials”. As a result, college principals in London were comparatively unfettered by national policy, and able to assert their personal stamp on institutions.3

 

European avant-garde influences

Evidently Johnstone was open to European avant-garde influences. In 1947 he was appointed at the Central. He adopted a policy of introducing painters into unexpected departments. The Fine Art staff included such figures as Robert Adams, Alan Davie, Anthony Gross, Richard Hamilton, Patrick Heron, Nigel Henderson, Roger Hilton, Paul Hogarth, Louis le Bocquay, Victor Pasmore, Eduardo Paolozzi, Mervyn Peake, William Roberts, William Turnbull and Keith Vaughan. Several of these (Hamilton, Henderson and Paolozzi) were members of the influential Independent Group, which met principally at the ICA. The architect Peter Smithson was also a member, and taught alongside Paolozzi. Reyner Banham was a member of the Art History staff. Geoff White recalls being taught at the Central by Victor Pasmore, Jesse Collins, Herbert Spencer and Anthony Froshaug. He believes the school very much followed the ethos of European Modernism and institutions such as the Bauhaus. The staff of the Furniture Design department included Robin Day, Frank Guille and Clive Latimer. The Architectural staff included numerous figures who became influential, such as Maxwell Fry, Jane Drew, Wells Coates, Denis Lansdun, Trevor Dannat, and the ex-students Peter and Alison Smithson.4 Johnstone claims it was he who recommended Drew and Coates to Le Corbusier, to work on Chandigarh.

 

Basic design courses

Johnstone was keen to introduce basic design throughout the School. Describing his experience at Camberwell, he says “In Britain during the 1930s basic design courses were started by Jesse Collins and Anthony Halliwell. While they were both influenced by Bauhaus teaching, they each brought new creative ideas to the subject”. Elsewhere, he describes how another Camberwell lecturer Edwin Straker introduced Pasmore to abstract painting (Straker worked in Halliwell’s department teaching basic design to ex-servicemen).5 Johnstone had a high opinion of Halliwell, having recruited him at Camberwell because he had been impressed by his work at Beckenham School of Art, where he had introduced basic design as early as 1933. Halliwell would have worked with Collins while teaching commercial art (ie graphic design). Johnstone suggests that it was due to Halliwell’s influence that Pasmore shifted from landscapes and cityscapes to abstract art, for which he is better known.6 During 1947, Halliwell was appointed in the School of Jewellery and Silversmithing and formed a course in Design for Light Industry. As a result, he and Johnstone were “at last able to put into effect those ideas we had dreamed about at Camberwell before the war”.7 They recruited Robert Adams, Bruce Archer, Nigel Henderson, and Robert Welch to the course.

He goes on to add that when he arrived, he was disappointed that Collins was not in charge of the School of Book Production. Collins was teaching only part-time, while also working with Misha Black and colleagues at Design Research Unit, which he opines “made a considerable impact on graphic design in this country” (see Chapter 5). While he admired Collins, Johnstone also respected the contribution made by previous members of the School of Book Production, such as Douglas Cockerell, Cobden-Sanderson, Eric Gill, Graily Hewitt, JH Mason and Edward Johnston. Several of whom had worked closely with both the Monotype Corporation, and Count Kessler’s Cranach Press in Weimar.

 

When ultimately able to appoint Collins as head of department, he describes him as “a splendid Head of his Department; he was also a fine and inspiring teacher who had, on occasion, a magnificent Irish temper”.8 They both had to engage in protracted negotiations with the print unions when seeking to introduce typographic design teaching to trade apprentices. Johnstone noted that “During the fifties, the very best students chose to study graphic design and typography rather than opt for the Fine Arts, which seemed to only attract third- or fourth-rate students”. He goes on to cite as examples of the former Colin Forbes, Herbert Spencer, George Daulby, Alan Fletcher, Peter Wildbur, Allan Ball, Derek Birdsall, Kenneth Garland, Peter Firmin and Mervyn Kurlansky. He continues by saying “That most excellent typographical designer Herbert Spencer told me once it was a very exciting place to be – the only place where there was an attempt to grapple with the real problems of industrial design”. This then was the environment in which many of the most inspiring designers during the post-war period met and interacted. We shall be profiling several of them later here

 


Post-war students

The country was experiencing a dynamic period with a vibrant socialist ethos. Many of the students were ex-servicemen returning with experience of serving overseas. Inevitably, they brought with them a greater maturity and a hunger for change more pronounced than with many undergraduate students today. One such was Ken Garland, who confirms that Johnstone was extremely good at identifying and bringing disparate staff together.9 As an example of the way in which Johnstone mixed staff from differing disciplines Ken cites Eduardo Paolozzi and Victor Pasmore, whom Johnstone insisted should teach basic design in the Textiles Department. He adds that Richard Hamilton, was “loquacious – ad nauseam”; and describes how students could “wander into” all departments. Geoff White confirms this, observing that he spent much of his own time in the Painting Department.

Of his time at the Central, Ken Garland says, “The atmosphere was enormously enthusiastic…We had a feeling that we were a generation of some significance…there was something to be done, there was a world to be made. It was definitely there, a feeling of building a new society”.10

 

 

The sentiment clearly was characteristic of many others. In Lucienne Roberts book ‘Drip-dry shirts..’ Colin Forbes says “I did my national service…got a grant…It was extraordinary; at the time, the Central was the place to be. William Johnstone, the principal, was an unreasonable, egotistical tyrant, but he really had a nose for talent”…11 “Reyner Banham, Henrion, Mervyn Peake, William Roberts, Eduardo Paolozzi were all brought in by Johnstone. Terence Conran, Alan Fletcher of course, Derek Birdsall were students – a new generation of designers came out of the Central”.12

 

Jesse Collins

In his book ‘Burning the Box of Beautiful Things’ Alex Seago attributes Collins success to the fact that “he was virtually unique amongst heads of British graphic design departments during the late 1940s because he was not an illustrator, a wood engraver, a calligrapher, or a printmaker, but a professional commercial graphic designer, one of the co-founders…of Design Research Unit.” He goes on to say “Collins was also unusual amongst contemporary British graphic designers in his appreciation of the modern movement in architecture, painting and design”.13 Robin Kinross’s account of Anthony Froshaug provides a very sympathetic account of Froshaug’s experience of having studied under Collins, and later working with him.14

Derek Birdsall says Collins; “was the kindest man and greatest teacher I have ever known (our youngest son is called after him). On my first day, he filled out my timetable in pencil on my index card. (I later realised that this timetable was written in pencil for a very good reason – if a class dropped below eight students, it was closed down. Students were sometimes asked to sit in classes dropping below eight to maintain them and the teachers – a benevolent conspiracy). After drafting my timetable Jesse said, “I’ll take you up to meet Mr Froshaug”.15

 

 

Ken Garland is on record as saying of Collins and Froshaug, “I suggest that their work in this department, notwithstanding the fact that Froshaug’s appointment lasted only for the two years 1952 and 1953,16 formed the true focus of teaching and thinking on graphic design in the vital five year period from 1951 to 1956; that it attracted the most forward looking and stimulating teachers on the subject”.17

He goes on to say, “Collins seems to have been as adept as Johnstone in attracting a stimulating group of staff, with complementary attitudes and skills”. Typical of these was Edward Wright. Ken Garland writes with enthusiasm about Wright‘s evening classes in experimental typography, which deserve “special mention”. He goes on to say “we used to have the most exciting fun pushing around large types, discarded halftones and anything that was type high, on an Albion Press under Wright’s benevolent and encouraging eye, saved (for a while, at least) from the outrage of the trade printers by the fact that we were doing our awful thing only in the evening, and by the authority of Anthony Froshaug, who waged god knows how many bitter battles with those narrow-minded little people on our behalf.”

 

 

“One marvellous aspect of those evenings was that many outsiders joined us there; Germano Facetti, an Italian trained as an architect who had arrived in Britain only two or so years before; Theo Crosby, an architect who launched ‘Uppercase’ magazine…Pat Crooke, an Architectural Association-trained architect; Don Hunstein, an American photographer; and Joseph Rykwert, a poet and art historian.”18 At the time, Theo Crosby was working for ‘Architectural Design’ and encountered Edward Wright when studying sculpture part-time. Robin Fior was another member of what must have been an animated group. Richard Hollis remembers Facetti being adept at picking the locks on equipment secured by the Printing staff, presumably having learnt the skill during his time in the Italian resistance.19

 

FHK Henrion influence on young graduates

Another figure who obtained his first teaching job in Collins’ department (in 1948) and later became well known was FHK Henrion.20 Subsequently, some ex-students returned to teach at the Central. They include George Daulby, Colin Forbes and Peter Wildbur. Both Margaret Calvert and Richard Hollis comment on George Daulby having made an impression on them.21 Several others went on soon afterwards to teach elsewhere, particularly at the London School of Printing and Graphic Arts. Many of Collins former students invigorated a later generation of designers through both their practice and teaching.

 

Photography

Strangely, photography does not appear to have been a prominent part of the curriculum of the graphic design course at the Central during this period. This is surprising, as the Reimann School had included an entire Photography Department, which included industrial and commercial photography as well as photo-journalism. The Reimann School had moved to London from Berlin during 1937, where it had been a much larger and prominent institution. The London school closed at the beginning of the war. It had included amongst its staff such figures as McKnight Kauffer, Eric Fraser, Milner Gray, Richard Hamilton and the documentary film maker John Grierson. Yasuko Suga completes her brief account of the school by featuring a project by Agatha Christie, who studied photography at the Riemann School.22

Moreover, Tschichold had written in both 1930 and 1931 in the British trade magazine ‘Commercial Art’ on the potential of photography in both print and exhibitions.23 His chapter in ‘Typographische Gestaltung’ on ‘Schrift und Foto’ (ie Type and Photo), with its wonderfully vivid examples, would have been known to both Collins and Froshaug. The latter would have known it well, as Robin Kinross’ includes a photograph of a room in Froshaug’s Cornish cottage during 1950 which shows a copy of Tschichold’s ‘berufsphotograph’ poster of 1938.24 Ken Garland describes how he discovered Nigel Henderson who “ran an unorthodox photography unit in a distant and largely overlooked corner of the Central School”.25 He recounts elsewhere that when Henderson recommended that he should study Moholy-Nagy, his response was “What is it?”.26 Geoff White refers to the photographic facilities being located within the Furniture Department, where they were used primarily not for their creative potential but for use in project reports and suchlike.

 

Attitude towards employment and the related profession

Collins was keen to assist his students in finding suitable employment. In the introduction to his book ‘notes on book design’ Derek Birdsall tells how “Jesse Collins sent me in a taxi with a job I had designed for one of the governors. As I got into the cab – one of the first I had ever taken – being 19 at the time – he said, ‘Remember that the client knows nothing of the work you have been doing during the last two weeks. Before showing him the job, take a minute or two – no more – to explain your approach. In that way, what he sees will not come as a surprise. It will be the natural outcome of your thinking’”. Similarly Ken Garland relates how Collins one day announced that he (Ken) was to be a magazine designer, and that he had arranged an interview for him with a potential employer.

Through his work in the department at the Central, it could be said that Jesse Collins was one of the most instrumental figures in Britain in developing graphic design as a concept. Johnstone observes that during his tenure he decided that the name of the department should be changed from ‘School of Book Production’ to ‘School of Book Production and Graphic Design’. He does not give a date for this, but the implication is that this took place during Collins’ tenure

Colin Forbes writes, “Jesse retired and Johnstone offered me the job of head of department in 1956 and I did that for three years”. He goes on to say, “I don’t think I was a particularly good head of department. I was at my best when I used to teach a typographic class, but teaching was not for me.”27

The Central continued to have an influence amongst former students, who for years continued to meet regularly on Friday evenings, at the The Lamb pub, in Lamb’s Conduit Street. More importantly, the relationships were manifest and varied between staff and students, staff and staff, and students and students. For example Colin Forbes and Alan Fletcher, and Theo Crosby were all students at the Central (though Colin and Alan may not have known Crosby at the time). Colin Forbes may have known Derek Birdsall similarly, though Colin may have been a member of staff when Derek was a student. Certainly, George Mayhew was a lecturer and invited former Central students Derek Birdsall, George Daulby and Peter Wildbur to establish BDMW.

Modernist Graphic Design in Britain 1945–1980
Ian McLaren and Tony Pritchard

‘Modernist Graphic Design in Britain 1945–1980’ was first published in hardback during 2024. As it sold out quickly the authors wish to broaden the readership in the education sector. In a series for Design Reviewed in collaboration with The Modernist Society, we will publish profiles of a number of lesser-known graphic designers featured in the book who helped shape Modernist graphic design in Britain during the post-war period. Coinciding with a second printing of the book in softback the series begins with an exploration of the work of a designer who embraced continental European Modernist design and helped develop the themes which make Modernism in Britain distinctive.

 

Dennis Bailey

Dennis was born on the South coast of England; and brought up in Worthing. He refers to being intrigued by amongst other things watching local signwriters.1 Before the advent of decals and laser cutting, signwriters used the brush. So one can well imagine that Dennis’s typographic sensitivity was informed from an early age by watching this essentially craft based skill. His parents were ‘not hostile’ to Dennis’s early interest in the visual arts and he attended Worthing School of Art. From Worthing Dennis graduated to the Royal College of Art during 1950, where he spent his first year in the Painting School, as did all of his colleagues at the time. There he was taught by John Minton, of whom he says “He was a very good tutor. He told me a lot of home truths. I started with the idea that I was the incarnation of Cézanne, but he soon brought me back down to earth! He was one of those rare people who can criticise constructively. He could instruct and enthuse you at the same time”2

 

 

Introduction

Dennis contributed to a widely diverse range of graphic design since the 1960s. When Ian McLaren returned to the UK from Germany and Holland during the very early 1960s he was struck by the elegance and inventiveness of his work. There was little to match it at the time, which has remained the case to this day.

 

Early experiences

On graduating, Dennis won a travelling painting scholarship, which took him to Sicily during 1954. On returning he produced book-jackets for Jonathan Cape, for which he was paid the typical going rate of £15 each; and illustrated a literary anthology for Ginn & Company. His attitude on graduating was typical of the time. He describes it as “I thought I’d get a job part-time teaching and although I didn’t want to be an artist in a garret I thought it would be something like that. You just knew there was no money to be made from illustration but you liked doing it, so if you got the occasional drawing in the ‘Radio Times’ or ‘Lilliput’ maybe an advertising agency would ask you to do some work occasionally. The College encouraged you to cultivate patrons and the main one was Jack Beddington”.3

Dennis’s experience of working for him was not favourable. Alex Seago provides a vivid account of Dennis’s reaction when required to redraw a project for him. He was told the figures “looked like chaps who’d been picked up for importuning in the lavatories in Piccadilly underground station. I stormed out into Mount Street almost in tears and thought God Almighty, there must be some other way to earn a living! Do I really have to listen to this crappy, patronising, pompous nonsense?”.4 At the time Dennis was already teaching part-time at Walthamstow and Croydon schools of art.

 

 

Magazine work

Much of his best output has been for magazines. His first experience of working on commercial magazines was while working in Zurich for Walter Herdeg on ‘Graphis’ during 1955.5 It was also his earliest experience of Modernist typographic design. He is said to have become interested in typography “because he hated the results when other people added type to his illustrations”.6 More than once he has described how he had been inspired by the experience of emerging from the station onto the streets of Zürich, where poster sites served as a gallery of current innovative Swiss graphic design. He was impressed in particular by Josef Müller-Brockmann’s work for cultural events. “I started to get very interested in Swiss typographic design. Müller-Brockmann, Karl Gerstner, and Max Bill…they were the first people in graphics that I had real enthusiasm for”. They were compelling because they were “based on rational structures, it was abstract…it didn’t undermine my personal work and it enabled me to combine art and graphics”.7 It is hard to believe Dennis when he says his interest in type was self-taught, while working on Graphis, where Herdeg was not an avowed Modernist.

 

Goldsmiths Company

On returning to London the architect Alan Irvine introduced Dennis to the Worshipful Company of Goldsmiths. He went on to produce exemplary work for the Goldsmiths Company from 1960 onwards, the first of which was for the ‘International Exhibition of Modern Jewellery 1890–1961’. They also worked together for various architecturally related clients, which involved Dennis in designing the exhibition graphics as well as the printed materials for a variety of clients. They continued a lifelong collaboration on many exhibitions, including trade exhibition stands for companies such as Pirelli, and Sharp Control Gears Ltd in the 1960s; which also featured Dennis’s illustrations. Later they worked together on major art exhibitions including: ‘International Ceramics’, for the V&A (1972); and an array of exhibitions of similar standing for the RA, including ‘Pompeii AD79’ (1976); ‘The Gold of Eldorado’ (1978); ‘The Horses of San Marco’ (1979); ‘The Cimbaue Crucifix’ (1980); ‘The Great Japan Exhibition’ (1981); and ‘The Treasures of Ancient Nigeria’ (1982).

 

When Ian first encountered Dennis’s work, he was struck by his ability to produce equally elegant and appropriate solutions for such a varied clientele. He remains impressed by Dennis’s ability to evoke so effectively the diversely different content required by the wide range he produced throughout his working life. While freelancing at this time Dennis became acquainted with Mark Boxer, Brian Duffy and Terence Donovan, whom he was to work with later on ‘Town’ magazine.

Disillusioned with what he called the trendy “tan carpets, Italian glass and Japanese lamps” in vogue at the time, he left for Paris, in part to work with the artist and designer Sandro Bocola on a film about American jazz musicians in Paris. While there he was tempted to work on what he describes as “a short-lived literary journal”. During a brief period Dennis gave ‘Olympia Review’ a refreshingly original appearance, using bold condensed sans-serif headings, with his customary mix of inventively cropped photographs, his simply and delicately executed illustrations, and contrasting these with strictly controlled body-matter.

 

 

Swinging London and Town magazine

Persuaded by stories of “swinging London”, and learning that ‘Town’ magazine was seeking an art editor, he returned and was offered the rôle by Michael Heseltine’s partner Clive Labovitch. The magazine had been art edited by Tom Wolsey, who was German born. Possibly because of this he was influenced by the trend-setting German magazine ‘Twen’, which Dennis described as “the only magazine that had really well-set type”.8 ‘Town’ made a splash, due as much to Dennis’s energetic design as its editorial content. Sometimes his own photographs and illustrations were featured. Writing in 2007, Dennis described how he enjoyed the working environment at ‘Town’. The results were a vibrant mix of commissioned photoshoots in unlikely locations, his own and others’ illustrations, and inventive collage.9  The magazine was typified by its direct but elegant covers; and inventive editorial spreads using young photographers such as Brian Duffy, Terence Donovan and Don McCullin. Despite attracting much attention it did not survive beyond 1967 when the ‘Sunday Times’ colour supplement started publication.

Dennis went on to work on a number of other magazines, These included the ‘AA Files’ for the Architectural Association (1982–2006); an annual survey for the Economist Group ‘The World in 1987’ starting in 1987 until 2015; and a variety of publications and magazine restyles for them. He worked also on the ‘RSA Journal’ for the Royal Society of Arts (1988); the ‘New Statesman’ (1996); and the ‘BMJ’ (1988–2005); as well as covers for ‘The Listener’. During 1987 he joined forces with the former Art Director at the ‘The Economist’, Mike Kenny to form Bailey & Kenny, working jointly with Dennis’s wife Nicola.

 

Later work

His later work included the design of numerous books and exhibition catalogues (many with related exhibition graphics and posters). They are all a delight. Other clients included the British Council in Iran; ‘British Cultural Festival’ (1977); for Phaidon – ‘Bonnard’ and ‘20th Century Composers’ (unrealised); for Merrell – ‘Francis Bacon’s Studio’ (2005), ‘Performing Architecture’ (2006), ‘Zaida Ben-Yusuf’ (2007) and ‘Sir John Soanes Museum, London’ (2009). For the Danish publisher Informations Forlag –‘Christiania’ (1979); for the Arts Council – ‘Le Corbusier’ (1987); and for Black Dog – ‘Trevor Dannatt: Works and Words’ (2008). His many catalogue designs include for the Royal Academy – ‘Pompeii AD79’ (1977); for the Arts Council – ‘Dada & Surrealism Reviewed’ (1978) and ‘Picasso’s Picassos’ (among many others). For the RIBA – ‘Carlo Scarpa’ (1973) and ‘Eileen Gray’ (1974); and for the Centre technique de cooperation agricole et rurale – ‘Terres et Vivres’ (1989); as well as several catalogues for the Anthony d’Offray Gallery including ‘Gerhard Richter: Mirrors’ (1991). In addition he designed annual reports for a number of major companies such as Consolidated Goldfields and London Merchant Securities. Those for NM Rothchild produced during 1991 and 1992 must have been amongst his most demanding typographic assignments, which did not prevent him from producing typically elegant results.

 

A natural draughtsman

Dennis was equally gifted as a natural draughtsman. Len Deighton, who was a student with him at the RCA, says “Dennis Bailey and Lewin Bassingthwaite were outstanding artists setting a standard of sensitive draftsmanship (sic) which I knew I would never equal”.10 It is hard therefore to believe Dennis’s claim that the only entire book he has illustrated was in 1954, the literary anthology for schools published by Ginn and Company, ‘Read to Write’. Of this he said it “was done well before I tried my hand at graphics”.11 A number of his illustrations have been included in book jacket commissions, notably with Derek Birdsall for the Penguin Education series. His fluid and natural illustrations have appeared numerous times on covers for ‘The Economist’; ‘The Illustrated London News’; ‘The Listener’; other Penguin Books; and Jonathan Cape. He also produced commercial illustrated work for magazines and for other design groups (such as Pentagram) and for companies which included Herman Miller.

 

 

Nicola Bailey notes that “At one time in the 1950s Dennis had considered architecture as a career, Hugh Casson even offering to sponsor him. While at Worthing School of Art he had filled notebooks with beautiful drawings of different architectural styles and local buildings. Throughout his career he worked with architects producing visual realisations of their projects though for some reason he never fully appreciated this ability, seeing it more as a means of earning a living. He could take sheets of plans and translate them into real places, often querying some of the architectural decisions where doors, walls and windows did not fit. Examples of this were his drawings of ‘The Globe Theatre’ for Theo Crosby and Sam Wanamaker in the early 80s; a Robert Adam interior relocated to the new Lloyds of London building for Pentagram (1985); and drawings of schemes for Paternoster Square for Arup Associates 1987; among many others”.12

 

 

Another example of his modest opinion of his abilities can be found in the Penguin Collectors ‘Penguin by Illustrators’ where he writes “Romek Marber, consultant to the stamp printers Harrisons commissioned me to design a set of four postage stamps for the ‘20th International Geographical Congress’. I thought no, this is not for me, I can’t do it. Romek pummelled and persuaded me. I, at one point, was pretty well camping in his studio. They came out well despite my doubts.”13

 

Royal Designer for Industry

In addition to his early teaching experience, between 1971–80 Dennis taught at Chelsea School of Art, when Edward Wright was the head of department. It was during his final year teaching there that the Royal Society of Arts recognised his long-standing contribution to design by awarding him Royal Designer for Industry (RDI). He died during 2016. Asked which of his projects he most enjoyed working on, he cited the catalogue for the exhibitions ‘Le Corbusier, Architect of the Century’ for the Arts Council (with its related poster); and ‘Hard Rain’ by Mark Edwards and Bob Dylan of 2006 (though sadly spreads from these do not reproduce well). His work is characterised by his combination of what appears effortlessly elegant typographic design, and equally fluent draughtsmanship. He was a charming companion and an exceptionally rare talent.

content.rendered:
This article is part of a series I will be adding to the website called Design Translated. Where I will scan and translate content featured in rare design magazines published between 1920 and 1940. Many of these texts have never been translated before. My goal is to offer fresh perspectives and shed light on forgotten information, designers, and imagery from this fascinating era.

This article was originally written in German and English and published in Typographische Mitteilungen, Vol 25, No 02, February 1928

Colourful posters, designed by artists and artistically inclined individuals in every conceivable style and fashion, produced in lithography and offset printing, now decorate walls and notice boards. All sorts of striking motifs and personalities are depicted in order to catch the eye, to arouse curiosity and entice people.

In contrast to this exuberance, the pure type poster—or one produced only with typographic material—however skilfully and richly arranged, often appears rather sober, even dull. Now the business of lithographic and offset printing is flourishing, but the book printer too may occasionally secure work, even if not always highly profitable. Invitations and admission tickets, programmes and costume emblems are required, and only the typesetter who approaches the task with imagination, vitality, and a lively, pulsating spirit will shape them successfully—one who has not merely observed carnival activity but has experienced and lived it.

 

 

 

He will seek to give these printed pieces the charm they require, at least making them more atmospheric than the sober observer and bystander. In designing such work, strict rules and regulations should not hinder the typesetter; here he must be able to work freely. The main thing is that the work appears interesting, appealing, light, and entertaining.

Of course, the materials available in the print shop must allow for such treatment. A welcome contribution is the silhouette ornament brought to market by the Ludwig Wagner type foundry in Leipzig, as well as the “Hamburg components” produced by the firm Genzsch & Heyse (Hamburg and Munich), and the decorative elements from the Stempel foundry in Frankfurt am Main. It would be desirable for this material to be expanded further. With these ornaments, the lightness of carnival motifs can be effectively composed.

A good method for working precisely with such material is as follows: the pieces relevant to a motif are lightly inked and arranged by hand on thin tracing paper; this provides a clear overview and makes it possible to shape the motif appropriately to the material. The composition can then be assembled quickly and efficiently. Another method, though more time-consuming, is this: the forms of the relevant ornaments (of which there are many) are drawn at full size on black paper or card and then cut out. These shapes are then arranged according to the motif and lightly mounted onto white card.

The work is worthwhile in that these paper pieces can easily be stored and reused for other purposes. Even by this method, work can be carried out quickly and reliably. In principle, however, one often hears complaints from type foundries that typesetters are not able to create anything clever with this material.

On the other hand, one hears from the typesetter: “Yes, now we have the ornaments, but we also need points of reference to know what can be done with them.” Who is to blame? Those responsible are often those who keep type and ornament samples locked away in cabinets and drawers, only occasionally showing them to customers, thereby giving a false impression of their capabilities. The samples should be displayed so that every typesetter and printer can access them; indeed, they should even be allowed to take them home for study—then the complaints would fall silent. To list carnival motifs would be pointless; one must experience, think, and observe for oneself—then one will find the right solution and be able to apply it in one’s profession.

 

 

 

Explore more on early twentieth-century typography and print culture through the archive. See related movements including New Typography and Bauhaus, and browse artefacts from Germany. You can also explore wider contexts in 1920s graphic design history and discover how typography and print evolved during this period. Browse the full Typographische Mitteilungen series to see more artefacts from this publication.

This article offers a rare insight into how typography functioned beyond the constraints of formal modernism, revealing a more expressive and atmospheric approach to printed matter.

Through these translated texts, I aim to surface overlooked perspectives like this, connecting designers, processes, and ideas that continue to shape how we understand graphic design today.

content.rendered:
A chance search on eBay for Henrion brought up an item I had never seen before — a portfolio and exhibition catalogue documenting the corporate identity work of Henrion Design Associates, dated 1971. I have previously profiled Henrion and documented the artefacts I had collected, though these were mainly his covers for Design magazine and a few others.

The catalogue offers further detail on the branding projects undertaken by Henrion’s agency, with translated commentary on each project alongside the visuals. I have gathered all the text and images below and hope to find more items like this in the future.

Introduction (1971)

Most people’s idea of design is probably that of making beautiful or useful objects — whether a potter making a bowl, or a whole factory making a car. The finished object is judged as “well-designed” or “badly designed” as if it existed in isolation, as if in a museum. We believe that some of the new and important problems in design are not to do with objects, considered in isolation, but to do with systems of objects, considered as a whole. We have therefore gradually developed a system approach to design.

A system is a collection of parts which work together to form a whole at a level higher than any of the parts. The whole system may outlive any of its parts; it may have needs, abilities, and a character different from any of its parts. The systems approach, when given a whole, looks for the parts which make it up, and when given parts look for the whole which they form. The systems approach looks at activities rather than objects, at change and development rather than the situation at a fixed time, at large numbers and probabilities rather than isolated cases. The systems approach is being usefully applied in many fields, especially where there is accumulated knowledge of parts as a basis for systems thinking in problems at a larger scale. It is characteristic of the systems approach that it calls for organised knowledge and techniques from several disciplines, for a team of experts co-operating on a new problem which none could solve alone.

The systems at the centre of our work are corporations, either business or governmental. Modern management is familiar with the systems approach in operational research and in general business consultancy. Our role is to extend this approach to the corporate image — the idea or appearance that the corporation presents to the many audiences it necessarily has. “The public” is not one but many potential customers, past customers, shareholders, staff, agents, competitors, the press, and so on.

All of these build up a picture of the corporation from what they see and hear of it. In many corporations the appearance overall gives a rather bad impression, usually because it has never been treated as a whole. A few good aspects are lost in a mass of poor, neglected, ones. The heart of a good image is a strong and clear identity. A corporation must be well-known and easily recognised by its audiences if it is to hold and improve its reputation. This becomes crucially important when a corporation either divides a known identity into several parts (as the British Post Office) or merges several identities into a larger group (as the Blue Circle Group) or interRent. The problems here are often caused by various conflicts and loyalty to the past within company management. People outside the corporation are usually quicker to welcome change, so long as it is seen to change for the better, and so long as it is clearly and strongly presented.

Perhaps the most striking difference between design of objects and co-ordination is the quantity of information which has to be processed, before, during and after the visually creative stage. In most corporations the idea of design management is absent — The design items are controlled by many different people at different places and with different levels of authority and ability, or left uncontrolled. It is necessary to collect information on the present situation before proposals can be developed. All this information has to be structured, filed and analysed, in collaboration with corporation management, in order to get a clear and factual working brief. During development of proposals, a large number of requirements usually have to be balanced, and possible solutions have to be optimised in several stages, again in collaboration with corporation management.

After proposals have been accepted, the implementation is always a large and complex problem, where time and cost have to be minimized, and effect maximised.

Some of the techniques we have developed for controlling this information in the preliminary, creative, and application stages are shown in the exhibition.

The need for systems thinking and coordination in design is growing, as corporate and social structures become more complex and faster-changing. In this exhibition we try/hope to show some of the ways to meet the challenge.

Ramon Blomfield, Margaret Ford, Patricia Ford, Terry Hanby, FHK Henrion, Peter Higgins, Norma Kitson, Stephanie Leigh, Helen Long, David MacIlwaine, Günther Murr, Alan Parkin, Roger Pemberton, Jane Sampson, Martin Sampson, Emily Teo, Terry Tyrrell, Marion Wesel, Trevor Whitmarsh, Jörg Zintzmeyer

 

 

KLM

A large corporation can rarely afford to make a sudden and complete break with its past, even if its management wishes to do so. KLM has an exceptionally widespread organisation, with stations all over the world. It is also among the oldest and best known of the international airlines. Market research showed that the initials, the crown and the stripes had well established recognition and goodwill value, but they were badly lacking in associations with modernity, which is very important for an airline. It was also known that the changeover period between old and new would be fairly long, to avoid the cost of withdrawing aircraft from service for repainting and wasting stocks of items in the old identity. For these reasons the proposals were to make the existing initials, crown and stripes more modern, strong and flexible. This was done by making the stripes horizontal, wider, and fewer; and by making the letters and crown bolder and clearer. The new set of elements is demonstrably simpler and stronger than the old.

The Crown was the subject of many studies, of which 15 are shown below. The ultimate form, which was disparagingly described at one early meeting as an “IBM Crown”, was after 12 months of presentations and discussions accepted as just what was needed to improve associations with modernity. Under poor viewing conditions — distance, movement, sharp angle, low attention — it becomes more crown-like, a result of the perceptual processes discovered by gestalt psychologists.

 

The new set of elements is demonstrably simpler and stronger than the old.

The system was made flexible by specifying a series of abbreviations of the full set of elements, from all-over stripes as on aircraft tails; To a rectangle of stripes, as on buses; to a rounded only, as on service vehicles; to initials and crown only, as on spaces with limited height; and exceptionally to letters only, where height is very limited.

 

We were recently asked to make a review of the identification system, for the Jumbo-jet era. This gave us the chance to go further than had been possible seven years earlier — to drop the stripes and rely entirely on the now well-established letters and crown, on a white ground.

 

 

 

 

Post Office

These proposals were the result of a three-year consultancy to the Post Office, involving many aspects of design co-ordination. Only the Giro symbol is in use.

The British Post Office has a long and distinguished history, and a very wide field of activities. At the beginning of this study it owned and operated all telephone equipment, and a banking service, as well as the range of postal services. The decision was taken that it should become two or more nationalised undertakings, instead of a single Civil Service. The need was for an identification system which would express the right balance of likeness and difference between these parts. The Giro symbol was developed and used before the other requirements were classified. Several identification systems were evolved, using symbols and colours, of which one set for four are shown opposite. These were for the Royal Mail, the Post Offices, the postal services, personnel, and transport by road, sea and air, (which may use the crown and the monarch’s initials), the telecommunications services, and the data processing services. By using one colour and different symbols, or one symbol and different colours, or different colours and different (though related) symbols, various degrees of likeness could be expressed according to the final management decision.

 

 

 

The general design co-ordination problem in the Post Office was very complex, with design items from pillar-boxes to stamps, telephones to public forms, controlled by departments all over the organisation with no central policy.

One of the first tasks in a design co-ordination programme is to gather information on the existing design situation, and to analyse it into a manageable form. This diagram summarises HDA’s survey for design co-ordination in the Post Office. Many interviews were held with members of almost every Post Office department, at all levels from director to executive officer, and with outside authorities who work for and with the Post Office. Every design item mentioned in these meetings was listed, according to the controlling departments, taking note of the other departments which have additional control or influence in each case. This gives the administrative control structure shown in simplified diagrammatic form at the left, which is in fact very complex and varied. The next step is to rearrange the design items in “design groups” — that is in groups which should be considered in relation to each other. This is in many cases quite different from the administrative grouping. For example, pillar-boxes, telephone kiosks, and stamp vending machines might be sited on the street side by side, and should hence be closely co-ordinated (even to the extent of considering a combined unit); but administratively these are controlled by three separate branches with no formal co-ordination. On the other hand, we felt that the design of “public information” should be more sharply distinguished from “promotion” than the administrative structure would suggest. The diagram shows the eleven design groups which we found sufficient to cover the design items.

Each design group contains a large number of items, as shown here for one group only. The dotted lines at lower left show our original proposal for design management in the Post Office. Instead of multiple separate control of design by non-specialist staff, we proposed a design administrator (DA) and a co-ordinating designer (CD) to manage design throughout the range of items. In initiating a project the branch responsible and any other branch affected would be convened with a designer and, where suitable, a manufacturer, to establish the brief. This group would develop proposals, with guidance as needed from the DA and CD. Longer-term research and design development should be set up as required. Approval of major projects and policy would be the responsibility of a design panel, a group with the high authority essential for successful design co-ordination.

A special study was made of possible telephone service developments up to 2000 A.D. resulting not in design of objects but in design of a modular concept or system (overleaf). The idea was to use standard functional modules so that as a user’s needs and technological facilities grew, modules could be added to this existing equipment, rather than installing a new object unrelated to the old. As miniaturisation is certain to continue, it was anticipated that each box could eventually take two or more modules. The modules shown are all technically feasible and most are in service or under consideration in some form or other. Only the co-ordination is new.

As of recommendations on a range of colours for telephone cases, the idea of a transparent case was proposed, and also gold and chromium electro-plated onto plastic cases.

 

Blue Circle Group

The parent company, The Associated Portland Cement Manufacturers, was formed in 1900, grouping several companies together. The sales company for this group, The Cement Marketing Company, was formed in the 1920s. The Blue Circle was used as a trade mark for the cement. The group had grown considerably especially since 1945, to become the largest cement manufacturers in the world and had diversified into other products. The various combined and conflicting uses of many identities — APCM, CMC, Blue Circle, and some 20 allied and subsidiary company names, became increasingly confusing and divisive. In 1966 we were asked to make a survey, and as a result we proposed unification of all presentation under a standardised blue circle symbol, with subordinate vertical identification of various parts where necessary.

The main classes of design items were packaging, stationary, vehicles, and signs. Control of these items was fairly decentralised, and the method of collecting information was to devise suitable questionnaire forms for each class, which were sent to all those in control of the various items. The resulting information was then analysed, and a considerably reduced set of designs made which covered all needs more economically than the existing uncontrolled varieties, with correspondingly greater unity and strength of effect. The applications were controlled by network techniques over a scheduled 3 years.

 

Programmes of variety reduction and resulting economy were carried out for the group’s 2000 road vehicles and 800 railway wagons, and the 300 different bags, drums, and tins. A complete modular sign system was created for cement works all over the world, both internal and external signs which numbered over 1000.

 

 

 

interRent

A frequent problem is the merging of companies with different histories and backgrounds, which to operate as one, need a unified identity. First a European rent-a-car network throughout Europe was created under the name of interRent, incorporating VW rent-a-car, SU Selbstfahrerunion, ITAL and others. A new memorable symbol had to be created in which the company title “interRent” was incorporated as a keyword to help the learning process of recognising the new symbol — logotype iR. To clarify this operation the new interRent is launched internationally throughout Europe at first incorporating SU and ITAL and where appropriate, next to VW rent-a-car. After this first phase, the component firms will be discontinued to carry on everywhere under a completely unified iR interRent symbol. Thus, nationally, there will be continuity with previous identities, whilst internationally the firm will be known from the outset as interRent only. The price lists below illustrate this phasing, also it will be repeated on transport, posters, illuminated signs, facias, uniforms and stationery in the same manner.

 

 

BEA

BEA is a good example of second-generation design co-ordination. In the late 1950s it was among the first corporations to control its appearance and general policy by a design manager and in detail by a design manual.

By 1967 it had become clear that on the one hand, the standards of competition had risen both among airlines and companies in general, and on the other hand there were inherent difficulties in using the old identification elements. The main proposals were:

1) to replace the red square containing small letters, by a logotype of long low shape, to make best use of the predominantly long low spaces on shopfronts, airport desks, buses and aircraft.

2) to replace the small, outdated, silhouette aircraft symbol by a national emblem, suggesting both the Union Jack, and a flight symbol.

Because of the high degree of design control and awareness in the corporation, it was possible to present a very strong and closely argued case for the change. And by careful planning the implementation was carried through rapidly yet almost entirely within normal replacement and repainting cycles, with over 100 aircraft, over 1000 vehicles, 183 buildings all over Europe. A two volume manual defines and controls the range of normal applications, under the supervision of a design manager. These pages show the main standards and instructions needed for the Trident aircraft. The manual contains a general drawing, with page references to colour and constructions for symbol and logotype, and reference to large working drawings available from the design manager.

Each of over 1000 applications is covered in a similar manner, in the two volumes of the manual.

 

 

 

Audi NSU

When earlier Audi Autounion AG and NSU became one legal identity, there was a need to create a new unified image of the new firm shown in the new logotype, specially designed, and applied to the whole range of stationery, literature system, packaging, transport, uniforms and particularly illuminated signs throughout the whole world. We demonstrate here just a small, but extraordinarily important problem connected with the sign program. For legal reasons, it was essential that Audi NSU should appear next to each other and not one below the other, with the result that on a projecting sign where widths are limited by regulations the words Audi NSU (seven letters) appeared markedly smaller than that of most competitors using only four or five letter names. To comply with these restrictions, yet be as legible as other manufacturers names and at the same time show an exceptional appearance to create attention we decided to shown the words reading vertically from the bottom to the top. The illustrations shown here are part of our presentation demonstrating the advantages of this proposal against the additional horizontal word arrangement.

content.rendered:
Joseph Binder was a pioneer of commercial modernist graphic design. Born in Austria, he initially trained as a lithographer and typographer. Binder later studied painting at the Vienna School of Arts and Crafts, and in 1924 established his own studio, Wiener Graphik, in Vienna. One of his first major clients was the City of Vienna’s Music and Theatre Festival, followed by numerous poster and logo commissions for clients in Austria and beyond.

In 1936, Joseph Binder and his wife, Carla, moved to New York and by the late 1930s, Binder won the poster competition for the 1939 New York World’s Fair, significantly expanding his reputation across America. Alongside his poster work, Binder was a prolific cover designer. His work appeared on numerous design and lifestyle magazines, including Women’s Home Companion, Fortune, Gebrauchsgraphik, Graphik, and Graphis. These covers translated machine-age aesthetics into refined Art Deco compositions and have become prime examples of American commercial modernism. They symbolised the technological progress, speed, and power associated with American industry and society.

content.rendered:
“Never before had modern printing been treated as a serious art whose province was to embrace the whole process from the selection and spacing of the type and the position of the printed matter on the page, to the embellishment of the book with appropriate initials and other decorative ornaments.”
Aymer Vallance
1899 issue of The International Studio

Art Nouveau is often described as the first international design movement. Although it manifested differently across countries, it shared a common ambition to unite art, craft, and industry. Its influence extended across multiple forms, from magazine covers and large-format posters to furniture, interiors, and architecture throughout Europe.

The movement was extensively documented in contemporary art and design magazines. Notable examples include the German magazine Jugend, which gave Jugendstil its name, the French publication L’Artisan Pratique, and Ver Sacrum, produced by the Vienna Secession and reflecting a distinct regional interpretation of Art Nouveau. Advances in print production and transportation made reproduction and international distribution significantly easier than ever before, allowing magazines to become one of the fastest and most effective carriers for the spread of ideas, styles, and visual information.

 

 

 

 

Alongside these publications, the early twentieth century saw the rise of trade unions, professional bodies, and design collectives that promoted shared ideals of good design. One of the most influential was the Deutscher Werkbund, founded in 1907. The Werkbund brought together artists, architects, designers, and industrialists with the aim of improving the quality of German design through collaboration between craft and industry. Its influence would prove pivotal in shaping modernist thinking and later developments in graphic design.

 

 

 

Within this period, new graphic languages began to emerge, most notably the reductive poster style known as Sachplakat (the object poster). Designers such as Lucian Bernhard rejected ornament and illustrative excess in favour of bold colour, simplified forms, and a direct relationship between image and message. This approach prioritised immediacy and clarity, reflecting the economic changes of mass production and the needs of a growing consumer audience. Graphic design increasingly became a tool for rapid communication.

These principles were later articulated in an issue of Commercial Art. Jan Tschichold, argued for efficiency, clarity, and visual economy in modern design:
“The speed of communication is today so great as to demand the utmost economy of statement and layout. We are obliged to aim at setting out our facts more simply and clearly to ensure instant comprehension, and at the same time designing our type to be more attractive to the eye and yet full of variety.”
Jan Tschichold, New Paths in Poster Work, 1931

His observations reflect a shift in design thinking, moving away from ornamentation and increasingly aligning design with function, speed, and reproducibility. These modernist ideas developed alongside earlier craft-led ideas of what art and design should be, offering an alternative value system rooted in making, ethics, and resistance to rapidly advancing industrial standardisation.

This emerging, systems-based approach to design stood in contrast to earlier philosophies rooted in individual craft and production. The Arts and Crafts movement, which arose in response to the mechanisation of the Industrial Revolution, sought to bring back the role of the maker within the production process. Believing that direct connection between designer and object, forged through handcraft, was essential to both human fulfilment and aesthetic quality.

Figures such as William Morris, often regarded as the central figure of the movement, championed moral responsibility in design and advocated for a return to craftsmanship. Morris largely rejected industrial production altogether, positioning it as a force that diminished both labour and artistic integrity, rather than something that could be reformed or harnessed through design.

 

 

 

Other organisations and professional groups and communities followed, including typographic and printing unions such as the Bund Deutscher Buchdrucker (BDB), the German Printers’ Association, The Nederlandse Typografenbond (Dutch Typographers’ Union), the American Institute of Graphic Arts (AIGA) and the International Typographical Union, alongside similar bodies across Europe that supported professionalisation, education, and the dissemination of design standards.

 

 

 

 

 

 

The First World War marked a shift in the role and purpose of graphic design, it became increasingly a powerful tool for propaganda, recruitment, and rapid mass communication. At the same time, avant-garde movements such as Dada, De Stijl, and Constructivism were emerging, challenging established visual conventions and pushing art and design toward new experimental and ideological directions.

The rapid progression of design, technology, and visual style during this period was recorded in design annuals and specialist trade journals. These included the British Penrose Annual, the German Das Plakat and Typographische Jahrbücher and Typographische Mitteilungen, and the Czech journal Typografia, all of which provide invaluable insight into evolving international practices. These became not just printed sources of inspiration but a place to test ideas, share opinion and educate and unionise.

Corporate identity began to emerge during this period as companies increasingly recognised the importance of a consistent and individualised professional visual language across their communications. A fine example is the work of architect and designer Peter Behrens for AEG (Allgemeine Elektricitäts-Gesellschaft).

Behrens was appointed as AEG’s design consultant in 1907 and is often credited as the first industrial designer. Whilst working with AEG, he developed a comprehensive visual identity system that included logo designs, advertising materials such as brochures, posters and catalogues, as well as product design. His work for AEG established a recognisable corporate image and laid the foundations for modern corporate identity practice.

During this same period, frameworks surrounding intellectual property were also established. The copyright symbol was introduced in the United States in 1909, signalling the growing recognition of authorship, ownership, and protection within publishing, design, and the wider creative industries.

It was not until 1922 that the term graphic design was first used. The phrase appeared in an article written by W. A. Dwiggins for the Boston Evening Transcript, marking a significant moment in the formal recognition of graphic design as a distinct professional discipline.

title.rendered: IBM, The IBM 3033 Processor Complex, Model Group N, c. 1978. Designed by Robert (Bob) Salpeter

content.rendered:
What began as a simple email thread quickly turned into a deep admiration for a designer whose name was new to me, Bob Salpeter. Since that discovery, his work has become a familiar presence in my archive, associated with a significant number of artefacts that span over a few decades.

When I think of the pioneers of mid-century to postmodern American graphic design, the first names that come to mind are Paul Rand, Herb Lubalin, Lance Wyman, Lester Beall, and Milton Glaser. I also think of companies with a strong design legacy like IBM, American Airlines, and CBS and the publications that provided the spread of graphic design like Print, Art Direction and Fortune.

But one designer who hasn’t received the recognition he deserves is Bob Salpeter.

 

My journey to discover and document his work began with an email I received from his daughter, Nina Salpeter. That message led me to archive, study, and celebrate his contribution to graphic design. His work reflects the spirit and advancement of American graphic design history from the 1950s to the 1990s and documents the change in materials, techniques and styles. He designed for sixty years, completing thousands of jobs.

Trained by Paul Rand at IBM and educated in New York, at the School of Visual Arts and the School of Industrial Art. Salpeter went on to build an extensive and impressive career. After he completed his studies, from around 1954 to 1957, he was a designer and illustrator for Ben Lorenz Associates and later worked on various freelance commissions.

From 1960 until 1971, Salpeter worked at IBM under the mentorship of Paul Rand. Rand remained one of his key influencers throughout his career alongside Bob Gill who taught him at SVA. He designed countless promotional materials for products and exhibits as well as internal communications. He utilised carefully selected paper stock for events and symposiums, providing the artwork of illustrations and designing sub-identities for events and communication areas.

This IBM Magnetic Character Recognition brochure was created in 1961, before Paul Rand created the IBM striped logo It’s ironic that the MICR had stripes, but the IBM logo at the bottom did not…yet.

 

 

These two program covers were printed on coloured, textured stock and have a real organic and sentimental feel.

 

In comparison this piece of marketing material features a striking modernist design that speaks of clean, digital, geometric design.

 

 

Salpeter also designed print material that was purely focused on typographic form and colour. This piece that he designed for IBM brings out key works in bold colours alongside the IBM striped logo.

Excelling in idea generation Salpeter was responding to briefs in a very bespoke manner, solving the needs and problems of a company, whilst maintaining the brand standards, that were set in place by Paul Rand.

His work was extensive, and his relationship with Paul Rand was not only professional but also as colleagues at IBM, but also personal. They remained close friends and even played chess together after his time at the company.

Unfortunately, Salpeter’s time at IBM was brought to an end when a mock-up of an advertisement was spotted on his desk, the ads copy ‘The IBM72 has something no other typewriter has. Balls.’, struck a nerve and the humour of the design was taken out of context, leading to his dismissal.

 

Whilst at IBM Salpeter was also teaching at Pratt Institute, passing on his knowledge to a new generation of designers from 1968 to 1971. The dismissal didn’t dampen his creative spirit, and after spending over a decade at IBM, Salpeter joined forces with Richard Lopez and founded Lopez Salpeter, where he was Creative Director. Lopez was previously an industrial designer with Walter Dorwin Teague. They worked perfectly as a duo, with Lopez’s technical background and Salpeter’s creative eye and experience in all things print.

“Sales is usually thought of as being diametrically opposed to design,” Lopez notes. “I had trained as an industrial designer, but discovered that the creative aspects of selling design really offered the most satisfaction to me.”
Print magazine, May/June, 1974

The company employed numerous designers and other staff to meet clients needs and to help with the design of corporate identities, films, posters and brochures, exhibits and annual reports. Their client list was extensive and included the American Museum of Natural History (for the Human Variation exhibition), the World Golf Hall of Fame (History of Golf exhibit), the American Cancer Society, Scott Printing, and IBM.

Lopez described their design philosophy in a 1974 Print magazine feature:
“We strive to give the client a solution that represents some thinking. Our solutions are pinpointed to specific needs. And we try to maintain a professional atmosphere of highly personalized craftsmanship.”

In 1979, he formed Salpeter Design and continued his working relationship with IBM, while attracting new clients such as  American Express, Sony, Goldman Sachs, and There’s no surprise, his work earned him numerous awards from organizations including the AIGA, ADC, TDC, and the Mead Library of Ideas. In 1978, he received a special recognition from AIGA’s Communication with Children exhibition for a film on DNA/RNA created for both the American Museum of Natural History and the Smithsonian Institution.

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

You can find selections of his work in Print magazine, Communication Arts and a few other design journals, I have a lot more images to scan and add of his work!

‘The solutions often communicate a cliché with a twist. A cliché, usually bad form, becomes useful because it is easy to understand. A twist freshens up the cliché.
A visual pun provides a new way to look at something and creates unexpected relevance.’

content.rendered:
1960 was a pivotal year in Japanese graphic design history. In May, Tokyo hosted the first World Design Conference, an event that reflected the growing public awareness of design as a profession and the recognition of its role in society. ‘The Conference aimed to promote international exchange with the global design community and introduce Japanese design overseas, becoming a major initiative that involved both political and business leaders.’

The year also marked a period of Japan’s rapid postwar economic growth, with the nation’s GNP rising to the second highest in the world. Mass production, mass sales, and mass consumerism, combined with advances in photography and printing technology, created the perfect conditions for the expansion of graphic design. ‘Japan blended Western techniques such as collage, montage, airbrush, and the International Typographic Style with traditional Japanese symbols, calligraphy, and aesthetics.’

At the start of 1960, the Japan Newspaper Advertising Association and the Japan Commercial Broadcasters Association launched the ACC (All Japan CM Broadcasting Union / 全日本CM放送連盟 / 全日本CM協議会), which coordinated advertising activity across the country. By March, the Nippon Design Centre (NDC) was officially launched, and later formally established in December by designers including Hiroshi Hara, Yusaku Kamekura, and eight companies.

Also in March, a design forum was established as part of the Tokyo Olympic Organising Committee, chaired by Katsumi Masaru and including Takeharu Imaizumi, Takashi Kono, Hiroshi Hara, Hideo Mukai, Kenji Ito, and Seiichiro Arai as members.

The Japan Design Student Union was formed in April and, a month later, held a student lecture series featuring leading global designers such as Herbert Bayer, Bruno Munari, Saul Bass, and others. In May, Tokyo hosted the World Design Conference, which was the first international design gathering in postwar Japan. The programme featured leading figures from across the globe, including Otl Aicher (Graphic Design in Advertising), Saul Bass (The Designer’s Responsibility for Visual Culture), Herbert Bayer (The Designer’s Position in Society), Max Huber (Contemporary Graphic Design and Society), Yusaku Kamekura (Katachi), Walter Landor (The International Style), Tomás Maldonado (Visual Communication), and Josef Müller-Brockmann (The Education of a Graphic Designer).

 

 

 

Throughout the year, graphic design gained further visibility through a range of exhibitions, including Japanese Design Perspective, World Graphic Design Exhibition, Design Education Exhibition, the Olivetti Exhibition, and the World Design Exhibition. A new organisation, the Japan Package Design Association, was also established.

By June, following a competition, Yusaku Kamekura’s design was selected as the official symbol mark for the Tokyo Olympics.

In August, the 10th Japan Advertising Artists’ Association Exhibition was held at the Mitsukoshi Department Store in Nihonbashi. Two months later, in October, the Japan Advertising Artists Club (JAAC) marked its tenth anniversary with an exhibition of members’ work.

This incredible year was documented in the Annual of Advertising Art in Japan 1960 (Bijyutu Shuppan Sha, 1960). The large volume is filled with some of the best advertising and printed matter from the year, and not only inspired me to write this article but also sparked my search for more original Japanese design for the archive.

Having documented and enjoyed two previous Italian design annuals, Pubblicità in Italia 1957-58 and Pubblicità in Italia 1959-60. I wanted to continue the series of documentation and gathering inspiration. ‘Pubblicità in Italia’ (‘Advertising in Italy’), published its first annual in 1953 and continued to be published until 1987. Each issue has almost 400 pages of inspiration and Franco Grignani designed all the covers. The annuals showcased the best of Italian graphic design and documented the changing language of advertising in a society that continually evolves.

Italy continued to expand its industry throughout the 1960s and consumerism was well underway. Many of the leading Italian companies were based in Milan such as Pirelli, Olivetti, Finmeccanica and Prada and although nearly all the designers are Italian, British designer Alan Fletcher designed a few Pirelli pieces that were featured in the annual.

 

 

 

Unlike the majority of design coming from Switzerland, Italian design still had a certain playful charm that blended with its modernist design, that’s not to say Swiss designers were restrictive, as you only need to look the work of Swiss designers, Celestino Piatti and Paul Trauffer to see the fine art and individual approaches they took to designing posters . But the brush strokes of Lora Lamm and Pegge Hopper for La Rinascente have a certain height of elegance and the Pirelli advertising by Pino Tavaglia that brings hand painted elements to an industrial product are fine examples of this. By comparing these scanned designs from the Swiss Poster Design award-winners, you can observe recurring approaches to typography and layout, as well as stylistic elements that become closely associated with each designer’s work. Pintori’s abstract compositions and brand language for Olivetti, Lora Lamm’s painted elements for La Rinascente and R. Manzi’s illustrated characters for Pirelli.

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

I am going to collect more of these annuals and document more Italian advertising in the postwar decades. It’s great to see the varying styles of photomontage, illustration, bold hand lettering, and photography.

The Bund Deutscher Gebrauchsgraphiker (BDG) was originally founded in 1919 and was the first professional association for graphic design in Germany. In 1949, after World War II, Chairman Eberhard Hölscher believed in the power of an annual poster competition, similar to the Swiss Poster Award. A year later, the competition began, with eight winning posters. 

The 13th annual poster competition included posters designed between May 1, 1961, to April 30, 1962. Of the many entrants (over 400 submissions), Gebrauchsgraphik 08, 1962, included designs by Karl Oskar Blase, Herbert Ludwig Bohrmann, Reinhard Braun, Walker Breker, Heinz Edelmann, Gerhard Eisenmann, Michael Engelmann, Fischer-Nosbisch, Harald Gutschow, Hans Hillmann, Herbert W. Kapitzki, Hans Kuh, Walter Landmann, Gerhard Lienemeyer, Hans Lohrer, Almir Mavignier, Hans Noeth, Klaus Oberer / Atelier Michael Engelmann, Hermann Rastorfer, Hans-Jürgen Rau, Eberhard G. Rensch, Günter Rambow, Richard Roth / Dorland Werbeagentur, Alexandra Sasulin, Hans-Jürgen Spohn, Erich Strenger, and Ernst Wild.

‘Today, at a time when the advertisement is the leading publicity medium one may quite justifiably ask why one had chosen the poster to serve as a cause and touch-stone for such artistic and publicity purposes. This choice was, however, an obvious one at the time, and it will become understandable when one remembers that the poster, due to its lively colors and impressive size, has of ever been the typical representative and the most popular of all pictorial publicity media. The results of those first competitions were admittedly not very encouraging since the submitted posters were uneven and fluctuating in quality so that, at the beginning only few good posters could be selected. This situation, however, rapidly improved in later years although far more critical standards were applied, and a considerable improvement of the artistic quality began to emerge.’
– Eberhard Hölscher – German Posters 1961/62

 

 

 

A lack of colour on the reproductions takes away from some of the works, but the designs still look incredible. A mixture of geometric clean work by Karl Oskar Blase and Walter Breker, to more illustrated and organic works of Hans Hillmann and Günter Rambow and Gerhard Lienemeyer. It’s incredible to think that over six decades on, many of these works hold up from both a typographical and illustration perspective and personally, I think many of these would be award-winning works today. Poster competitions and other design awards provide a benchmark for quality design and promote the profession to both companies and individuals. Society benefits from good design, and highly crafted work can remind us of the importance of good design and its benefits to the public.

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

The excellent general level of achievement and the great number of truly outstanding individual designs make it evident that the German poster art has rapidly flourished in recent years and stands comparison with even the best foreign designs.
– Eberhard Hölscher – German Posters 1961/62
