content.rendered:
The Bund Deutscher Gebrauchsgraphiker (BDG, Association of German Commercial Artists) held its 14th annual poster competition in 1963. The organisation was founded in 1919 and was Germany’s first professional association dedicated specifically to graphic designers and commercial artists. It played a central role in shaping the profession in the first half of the twentieth century, giving designers a platform at a time when graphic art was still fighting to establish its legitimacy alongside fine art and architecture. The BDG promoted design across all outputs, including advertising, posters, typography, packaging design, and illustration. As well as running its awards, the group organised exhibitions, ran professional meetings, and produced publications that helped German design gain further international recognition. Germany also published many leading publications for the sector!

 

 

Of the large quantity of posters submitted to the 1962/63 competition, 23 were chosen as the winners. As with many of the winning entries from earlier and later years, posters commissioned by film distributor Atlas Films won multiple awards, reflecting the strength of cultural design during this period. Many of the award-winning works came from the cultural and entertainment sectors, such as theatre, film, and festivals, while there was a noticeable lack of industrial or commercial posters. The selection suggests an overall feeling of individualisation among the designers, with varied styles and approaches, and in many cases, a restrained use of colour. In Gebrauchsgraphik, where a lot of the images were reproduced in black and white, this sense of limited colour usage was even more apparent.

The author of the article, Eberhard Hölscher (a long-time editor and critic for Gebrauchsgraphik), commented on this tendency, observing:
‘But what we are missing this time is a certain joyous verve and that touch of humor which formerly made our German posters so stimulating and optimistic. Last but not least we wonder why there is such an evident prevalence of one-colored designs. It seems that one has forgotten in Germany that it has always been colors which imparted to the poster its strongest effect and greatest attraction.’

 

 

 

 

 

I agree with Hölscher’s remarks to an extent, especially when comparing different examples in my own collection. I own both the Die weiße Taube poster designed by Lothar Städler and Die Liebenden von Verona by Hans Hillmann. While these show a certain lack of colour, the use of colour in Hillmann’s Die Sieben Samurai or the striking Ballet Festival of the Bavarian Staatsoper München poster by Hans Kuh demonstrate how essential colour could be to the impact of a design. At the same time, I feel both the Renault poster and the theatre poster designed by Hans Förtsch and Sigrid von Baumgarten prove that colour is not always necessary.

 

 

 

The 1962/63 prize-winning posters were judged by a professional jury and included works by many of the most notable German designers Hans Küh, Hans Michel, Günther Kieser, Reinhart Braun, Anton Stankowski, Herbert W. Kapitzki, Almir Mavignier, Hans Peter Hoch, Helmut Lortz, Hans Noeth, Michael Engelman, Lothar Städler, Hans Hillman, Walter Breker, Heinz Kröhl, Hans Förtsch and Sigrid von Baumgarten, Ernst Wild, Wolf D. Zimmermann, Hermann Rastorfer and Karl Oskar Blase. Their combined output illustrates the strength of the German design scene at the time, with an impressive list of established names and also younger talents.

Over the entire history of the BDG poster awards, which ran from 1949 to 2000, almost 4,000 designs were submitted. I hope to continue expanding my own poster collection, not only to study this history more but also to preserve it, adding examples of the posters as physical artefacts alongside the scanned material that already forms part of the archive.

content.rendered:
Following on from my previous article on publicity design from 1957-58, an additional annual from 1959-60 showcases another year of great design from Italy.

European graphic design in the late 1950s made a noticeable shift from more playful, ornate styles toward more regimented, structured, and direct forms of advertising. Illustrated campaigns were still common and adorned many walls and printed literature, but the spread of affordable televisions, faster and cheaper transport, and advances in production techniques created new demands. In a world increasingly defined by speed, advertising needed to deliver its message with clarity and immediacy. Designers sought to strike a balance as communication had to be both practical and expressive; it had to combine functionality with a strong graphic impact. Very much is the case today.

Vittorio Sereni, writing in Pubblicità in Italia 1959–60, reflected on this:
“The old advertising design was more gentle, something like an ornamental accessory offered to the consumer for the pleasure of his eyes; whereas the advertising factor is now located in a nevralgic point of the connection between production and sale, almost as a confirmation and an external and perceptible symptom of a circulation perfectly regulated between the two sectors.”

This tension between ornament and functionalism had already been observed decades earlier. In 1931, Jan Tschichold noted in Commercial Art:
“The speed of communication is today so great as to demand the utmost economy of statement and layout. We are obliged to aim at setting out our facts more simply and clearly to ensure instant comprehension, and at the same time, designing our type to be more attractive to the eye and yet full of variety.”
— Jan Tschichold, “New Paths in Poster Work,” 1931

 

 

 

 


Pubblicità in Italia 1959–60 featured a wide range of documented Italian graphic designers, alongside a few whose full names I have yet to trace (an area I will continue to research as I document more design history). As with many publications of the time, the list is dominated by male names, though it also includes the outstanding contributions of female designer Lora Lamm. Much of the advertising in this annual is as attractive today as it was in 1959. It still has examples of playful brush strokes like the work for Cinzano, but it’s limited against countless uses of sans-serif typefaces, visual cues and product photography.

 

 

 

 

 

 

Design for companies such as Pirelli, Olivetti, and La Rinascente continues to be a focal point in books about Italian graphic design, but looking through magazines from this time and the 1960s and similar annuals, you can’t help but notice a huge investment in leading designers from the pharmaceutical industry. Both German and Italian pharmaceutical firms seem to have recognised the importance of graphic design not only to appeal to contemporary audiences but also to safeguard and project their brand identities into the future.

content.rendered:
In 1964, Gebrauchsgraphik (issue 08) featured a selection of posters from the 1963/64 Die besten Plakate des Jahres (The Best German Posters of the Year Awards). Organised by the Bund Deutscher Gebrauchsgraphiker (BDG, Association of German Commercial Artists), the annual competition selected 22 outstanding designs. The award-winning works represented some of the most effective and stylish posters of the year, many of which remain visually striking today.

Founded in 1949, Die besten Plakate des Jahres became a leading platform for displaying and promoting German graphic design. It was established and overseen by the BDG, which was founded in 1919 by Max Hertwig, Jupp Wiertz, and Hans Meyer as the first professional association for German designers. Over the year, the BDG brought together a member list of influential figures, among them Albrecht Ade, Hans Peter Hoch, Herbert W. Kapitzki, Paul König, Hans Lohrer, Almir Mavignier, Hans Schweisse, Fritz Seitz, Anton Stankowski, and Kurt Weidermann.

The 1963/64 prize-winning posters were judged by a professional jury and included works by Walter Tafelmaier, Heinz Edelmann, Hans Michel and Günther Kieser, Hanswerner Klein, Harry Süchland, Fritz and Dorothea Fischer-Nobisch, Günther Rambow, Gerd Lienemeyer, Michael Engelmann, Erich Strenger, Hans Kuh, Hans Hillmann, Reinhart Braun, Hans Jürgen Spohn, Karl Oskar Blase, Theo Kittsteiner, Ernst Post, Richard Roth, and Gerd Grimm. Together, these designers reflected the diversity and ambition of postwar German poster design.

 

 

 

The competition also highlighted a broader tension in design discourse. 

‘‘Apart from some very insignificant exceptions, almost all posters pursue a commercial purpose. This also applies to the posters for theaters, movies or similar artistic performances, which are commonly given a cultural aura. At bottom, they have no artistic ambitions at all but just want to attract the crowd: to the box offices. They are purely commercial posters. When a classification is to be introduced, there is only the big category of those posters which serve commercial purposes and besides the very small group of other posters pursuing some ideal end. Let us consider this year’s prize-winning posters from this point of view. The selection meets our approval, and the German graphic artists have proved that they do know their job. Among the 22 posters as many as 19 can truly be called commercial posters, all the more since 6 of them actually advertise real « branded articles». The remaining 3 posters pursue ideal purposes, so the posters against exaggerated smoking, the poster for civil defence or that of the protestant church. No poster, however, will be found that pursues an exclusively cultural purpose.’  Gebrauchsgraphik 08, 1964

 

 

 

 

 

 

Even during times of political upheaval, Germany continued to develop, innovate, and push boundaries, shaping not only national identity but also the advancement of European graphic design. For a broader exploration of this history, Jen Müller’s Pioneers of German Graphic Design (Callisto Publishers, 2017) offers a fantastic overview.

I have a few of the Atlas film posters that were part of the winning entries, and I hope to expand my poster collection over the next few years.

title.rendered: Tony Mottola – String Band Strum-Along, Command Records, New York, 1962. Cover design by George Giusti

content.rendered:
Adding to my small collection of record sleeves provides inspiration at an affordable price. I’ve previously written about Command Records and their art director, Charles E. Murphy, who designed over eighty covers throughout his career. As a commissioner of record sleeve artwork, Murphy also commissioned Italian designer George Giusti to illustrate several of the label’s releases.

George Giusti was a graphic designer, sculptor, and architect with an illustrative style that blended mixed media, typography, and playful imagery. He began his education in Milan at the Reale Accademia di Belle Arti di Brera, later moving to Switzerland to work as a designer.

He opened his own practice in 1930, and between 1939 and 1940 worked on the Swiss Pavilion for the New York World’s Fair. After completing the project, he chose to remain in the United States. He was one of several notable Italian designers who relocated to mid-century America, including Leo Lionni, Albe Steiner, Bob Noorda, and Massimo Vignelli.

When the Second World War broke out, Giusti began designing publicity materials for the U.S. government, as well as a series of posters for the Museum of Modern Art.

 


During the 1950s and 1960s, his work appeared on the covers of Graphis, Modern Packaging, Fortune, Holiday, and others. He was commissioned to design both the covers and interiors of books, as well as album covers for labels such as Command Records.

 

 

 

His artwork was featured on around forty releases for Command, complementing the work of other designers like Josef Albers, S. Neil Fujita, Rudolph de Harak, and Charles E. Murphy. However, Giusti’s covers stood apart from the more structured, geometric abstractions of his peers. His visual language was freer, more emotive and personally more expressive than restrained.

His loose brushwork captured rhythm and flow from the music itself. Each cover was unique, not part of a series, but a visual response to the release it accompanied. Even sixty years on, these albums remain striking and inspirational, far more longevity than the photographic covers, that are rooted in the fashions and styles of their time.

I hope to add more of these covers to the archive and definitely more artwork by the great George Giusti.

title.rendered: Roland Calendar 1960, Roland Offprint, Offenbach, 1959. Illustrated by Klaus Winter + Helmut Bischoff

content.rendered:
Klaus Winter and Helmut Bischoff created beautifully illustrated children’s books such as The Sun, The Happy Owls, and The King and the Parrot and also designed advertising artwork for pharmaceutical products and printing inks.

I was fortunate to come across a selection of their illustrated numbers on AbeBooks, each one individually crafted for Roland Printers in 1960. The set includes thirty-one coloured prints. A lucky eBay search also led me to a copy of The Sun, which I picked up for just a few quid.

 

 

 

 

Klaus Winter was born in 1928 and Helmut Bischoff in 1930. Both Winter and Bischoff studied graphic art in Karlsruhe and at the Bauhaus in Weimar (later the Academy for Architecture and Fine Arts). It was during their time in Karlsruhe that the two met and, in around 1951/52 (two articles suggest each date), went on to establish their own studio in Offenbach am Main, Germany, called Winter+Bischoff.

They worked with clients both locally and internationally, earning several awards for their work. Their commissions included posters for the pharmaceutical industry, advertising for manufacturers of wallpaper, ink, and paint, as well as advertising and illustrations for machine manufacturers, publishing houses, tourist agencies, and the German Federal Railways.

For Roland Offsetmaschinenfabrik Faber & Schleicher AG they created they created 31 loose sheets of decorative numerals, all different and designed according to their individual characters, ‘giving users a fresh and different effect each day’. The sheets were printed by offset-litho in six colours and were designed using a variety of traditional art techniques.

 

 

 

 

 

What’s particularly interesting about their approach to design is how they worked together on each piece, creating a unified style that blends their individual, handcrafted techniques together.

‘Each making his personal contribution to the sum total of their work. This conception fits Winter + Bischoff very well. Yet they also display a kind of collaboration in which the results look as though they were the work of one personality. They discuss their commissions as individuals and thus pool their ideas. But as soon as they have reached agreement about the formal principles to be applied and the technical methods of execution, each one works on each detail: there is no division of responsibility.’
Graphis 102, 1962 (Hans Adolf Halbey)

Winter + Bischoff’s work blends fine art and graphic design and is a fine example of commercial design featuring a heavy use of stylistic illustration. In fact a lot of German graphic design in the 1960s has this strong relationship of commercial and professional typographic layout with the roughness and organicness of art. Especially other designers I have documented, such as Hans Michel and Günther Kieser, Michael Engelmann and Fischer-Nosbisch
